📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

Recent findings suggest that when a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

Recent findings suggest that “Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they noted in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”.

This is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or launched soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

In a recent development, the researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

According to recent reports, starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers stated. “New satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”.

Industry observers note that in 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Significant Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the matter,” Coss indicates. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Recent findings suggest that several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare looks from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Recent findings suggest that romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

It has been revealed that the Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance strategy in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me newly introduced appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

Recent findings suggest that “The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss states. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms. They have also been used by Indigenous Mesoamerican and South American peoples for centuries to induce visions. Though it was once thought that mushrooms were either magic or poisonous, there is one newly discovered species that, because of a bizarre turn in evolution, produces both psilocybin and lethal amatoxins, possibly as a defense against being eaten. That’s one trip you never want to take.

Galerina indica looks unassuming. Growing on rotting palm trunks in the humid swamps of Florida, this tiny brown mushroom has no fairytale spots or fantastical colors, so it seems like just another fungus bound to be stepped on. Under its dark cap is a darker reality. Matthew Smith of the University of Florida is the state’s official mycologist, identifying species that could be toxic and regularly consulting with Poison Control, and his team was searching for potentially lethal mushrooms when undergrad researcher Andrew Kunik noticed something strange. While documenting fungi, he found that handling G. indica turned it blue. This often occurs in psychedelic mushrooms. Further investigation found that, despite having this telltale characteristic, the mushroom Kunik had been analyzing had a more sinister kind of magic.

“Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, stated in a study recently published in Current Biology.

Sources indicate that while G. indica did contain psilocybin, it turned out that the ‘shroom also secreted deadly amatoxins. There is no other species of mushroom known for producing both of these substances, and while trippy psiloids have been shown to have possible therapeutic properties, ingesting amatoxins is fatal because these peptides inhibit the enzyme RNA polymerase from creating RNA copies of genes, which leads to organ failure. Fungi are thought to have evolved to produce amatoxins in order to ward off fungivorous creatures such as snails and nematodes. The genes behind production of both psiloids and amatoxins are usually passed down through fungi to their descendants, but the way these genes are acquired is not always so straightforward. Previous studies have suggested they can be horizontally transferred between different fungal species.

Industry observers note that psiloids are known to be synthesized by a cluster of collaborative genes for which evidence of horizontal gene transfer has been found. The same is suspected of amatoxin synthesis, and though there is less evidence for horizontal transfer, it probably began with a fungal donor lineage (which may not have been the same species) that has yet to be identified. Genome analysis has shown that these and other fungal attributes were acquired by genes that were transferred from one species to another growing in the same vicinity. The genus Galerina is already infamous for amatoxins that make many mushrooms within the genus so deadly. How psiloids entered the genus remains a mystery, though just one fateful transfer could have incorporated the genes for amatoxin synthesis into these mushrooms.

Industry observers note that what evidence does exist for the transfer of genes that produce psiloids suggests they seeped into a lineage that did not already contain amatoxins, and in a separate evolutionary event, was absorbed by a separate toxic lineage. Kunik’s discovery also revealed how unpredictable fungi can be. The blue pigmentation that is known to be a sign of a magic mushroom comes from psilocin oligomers, molecules linked together from a few repeating structural units, or monomers. Galerina indica has shown that seeing blue does not always mean a mushroom only contains psilocin or psilocybin. While the exact genes that are responsible for amatoxins in this species are still unidentified, and exactly how psiloids evolved in the Galerina genus can only be hypothesized, there is now another thing in Florida more dangerous than alligators.

“G. indica brings together in a single species the biosynthetic systems associated with both ‘magic mushrooms’ and the world’s deadliest poisonous mushrooms,” Kunik and Smith said, “providing a rare natural system for studying how horizontally acquired secondary-metabolite pathways impact organismal fitness.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

According to recent reports, “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

Sources indicate that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

Recent findings suggest that he continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a fresh life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

Recent findings suggest that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

Industry observers note that as he remarked, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

According to recent reports, then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

According to recent reports, mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

In a recent development, “Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

Breaking: The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity.
  • Sources indicate that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

Sources indicate that for almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

Industry observers note that but giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” indicates Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

In a recent development, the first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

It has been revealed that that thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

According to recent reports, inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

According to recent reports, the higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson indicates. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

In a recent development, englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

In a recent development, he and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also indicated that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their fresh masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work highlights. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

It has been revealed that “I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott claims. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

Recent findings suggest that most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he states. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

Recent findings suggest that fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher notes. “And he’s been struggling.”.

Sources indicate that perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales at the moment in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a latest masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Recent findings suggest that fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he claims.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

In a recent development, researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a upcoming masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

Sources indicate that such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

Sources indicate that however the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.

Tech Report: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they stated old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they stated old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from latest software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin stated “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

Sources indicate that “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin remarked. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Industry observers note that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

Sources indicate that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

It has been revealed that the committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a upcoming one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., stated in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications concerns.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell stated.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and remarked their committee would “thoroughly review the problems that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

Sources indicate that at problem in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have mentioned they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached.
  • Industry observers note that now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Emily Conover and Kathryn Hulick.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Industry observers note that now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge mentioned he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

According to recent reports, by the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

According to recent reports, A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as crucial as this,” claims mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

In a recent development, importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

According to recent reports, over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

In a recent development, the result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”.

According to recent reports, the Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis notes that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Sources indicate that because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”.

According to recent reports, AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”.

Sources indicate that kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra notes. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”.

The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

📅 09 Nov 2021 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a major snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it.
  • It has been revealed that electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects.
  • Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a major snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snowblower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

It has been revealed that electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with latest models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Ego Power+ 21-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower.

Sources indicate that ego claims this single-stage snow blower is able to clear a 14-car driveway on a single charge. Plus, it has heated handles.

Ryobi 21-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower.

Recent findings suggest that ryobi’s latest single-stage blower comes with two 40-volt, 8-amp-hour batteries for long runtime. It also has a tall clearing depth of 11.5 inches.

Wild Badger Power 20-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower.

We’re checking out this single-stage budget option to see if it can achieve effective snow removal for a small property.

Ego Power+ 24-Inch Two-Stage Snow Blower.

This is Ego’s latest two-stage blower, which we’re evaluating to see if it can hold its own against a gas-powered two-stage snow blower.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-amp-hour batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

According to recent reports, our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

It has been revealed that unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Industry observers note that combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear a 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

It has been revealed that ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

According to recent reports, like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

It has been revealed that since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime of up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Industry observers note that operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn swiftly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

Sources indicate that the e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

Sources indicate that we tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

In a recent development, to facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

According to recent reports, the chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

According to recent reports, dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That noted, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

In a recent development, throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to blueprint when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Industry observers note that snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Industry observers note that most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Recent findings suggest that though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

Industry observers note that “Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”.

According to recent reports, they’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most crucial thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

It has been revealed that if you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Industry observers note that most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you strategy to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

In a recent development, that mentioned, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

  • Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, as if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

Industry observers note that researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as big cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

Industry observers note that “It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” claims Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter notes.

“I found the evidence pretty compelling,” notes Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

According to recent reports, the eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter says.

According to recent reports, the eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter notes. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

In a recent development, the threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter indicates.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that some toys are timeless. From monster trucks that power over boulders to speed demons that clock 70 miles per hour, RC cars can thrill anyone who gets a controller in their hand for hours on end. Whether you’re an experienced driver looking to splurge on a higher-end model, a beginner looking for a newly introduced hobby, or a parent just trying to get your kid off the iPad, remote control cars are a great toy for all ages.

If you’re newly introduced to the RC world, shopping for a car (or an RC airplane, boat, or truck, for that matter) may feel somewhat daunting at first. It can get surprisingly technical, especially if you're looking at the hobby-grade cars. It helps to, at the very least, know how to tell the difference between the cars made for competitive racing and off-roading, detail-oriented models for collectors, and the more affordable options for kids and beginners. The good news is that while there may be a bit of a learning curve, you can get a taste of the action no matter your budget.

For more great toys kids of all ages are sure to love, check out our picks for the best remote control toys, the best drones, and the best robot toys.

Our testing focused on key features that factor into an RC car's day-to-day use, including speed, power, battery life, and handling. We drove a collection of cars on both flat indoor surfaces in our office, over uneven, hilly outdoor areas in New York’s Central Park, and through the fall foliage and around a tree-lined backyard in upstate New York. In addition to the basics, we measured the cars' acceleration, how quickly each car responded to radio signals, and checked the range of the remotes. We also took general notes on how easy it was to get the cars up and running.

Recent findings suggest that there are two models on this list we haven't tested: the Bezgar Off-Road Monster Truck and the Tamiya Nismo R34 GT-R Z-Tune. We recommended them after reviewing user recommendations and enthusiast reviews to find cars that represented certain areas our test units didn't fill. Our research spanned a range of different vehicle types from reputable RC brands, including Traxxas, Laegendary, Redcat Racing, and Bezgar.

Industry observers note that across the board, we wanted to make sure this list represented a wide range of RC cars, including options at several price points. Our picks include toy cars that cost $50 or less, mid-range RC cars under $200, and a few pricey models for experienced adult enthusiasts that cost as much as $350.

According to recent reports, in our latest patch, we performed additional testing on our existing recommendations, as well as a few upcoming cars. We also removed one recommendation, the VR Real Racer, as it has been out of stock for several months.

According to recent reports, the Traxxas Stampede RC car is our top choice because it combines speed, handling, and power better than any other option we tested. Its oversized monster truck tires aren’t just for show: They provided great traction and grip on dirt and rocks, as well as concrete and linoleum. Even compared to more speed-focused cars, the Traxxas brings some notable zip.

What impressed us most, though, was the handling. Even on uneven grass and dirt, we felt comfortable making sharp turns and precise movements at high speeds and the vehicle didn’t topple over. And it handled crashes like a champ: It took a few accidental head-on collisions into trees and fell as much as three feet off some rocks in the park and was no worse for wear.

Another key distinction for this RC car was how responsive and powerful the suspension was. Driving on bumpy surfaces and through dirt never swayed or threw it off course. The suspension made it easier to perform short jumps over ramps and ledges without crashing or damaging the vehicle.

It has been revealed that this well-priced off-road monster truck has working roll bar headlights, a spare tire attached to the back chassis, and an aluminum body that handles collisions at the truck’s top speed of 12 miles per hour. Its feature-rich design is an excellent value for beginners and experienced RCers alike.

In a recent development, the two-wheel-drive remote-control car is on the smaller side, at 1/14th scale, but it has a powerful motor to keep it rolling for up to 20 minutes on its all-terrain tires. The 2.4 GHz remote works from a distance of more than 160 feet away.

While it isn't quite as powerful or durable as our top pick, it serves as a perfect on-ramp to hobby-grade RC, giving you more oomph than a cheap toy.

If you’ve got a love for model cars, this is the right RC car for you. This scaled-down Ford Bronco is the near spitting image of the real thing, minus the less-than-ideal gas mileage. This miniature has grippy tires that match its slow but powerful motor. Just like the real thing, this Bronco climbs over rocks and rallies up inclines with ease.

Industry observers note that we tested the car going up large boulders in the park, and while it never zoomed over them, it continued moving effortlessly. We, of course, love the accurate exterior shell, but also found the interior body to be quite impressive.

The TRX-4M has a flexible frame and suspension system that allows for easy climbing on uneven surfaces. It comes with two headlights which, when the Bronco shell is snapped on, only further adds to the look.

You can grab one of these RC cars in multiple colors, including blue, orange, white, red, and black.

Recent findings suggest that if you want speed, try out this LaTrax Desert Prerunner racing truck. While it may not win you any competitive RC races with professional builds, this is a hobby-grade car with some serious juice behind it for its size. Driving it around required a bit of adjustment time because of its quick acceleration and sharp turning radius, but that’s exactly the type of challenge we love to tackle.

Recent findings suggest that the grippy tires and bouncy suspension also meant that this car picks up some serious speed outdoors. We drove it over hills and through rocks without losing any speed in the process. We loved the way it spins and drifts when it has some dirt or gravel underneath it and found ourselves trying to spin it around trees for fun.

It has been revealed that the car, much like other Traxxas products, is also quite durable. It handled a few spills and wipeouts with no real damage to the body or motor. That stated, be careful driving it through leaves and sticks because we found several accumulated under the outer shell after our drive.

According to recent reports, many of the RC cars we tested are off-roaders with thick tires, grippy treads, and bouncy suspensions. This allows them to drive promptly and responsively across tons of different surfaces like dirt, gravel, grass, and up rocks. This model from Tamiya is designed for the exact opposite: It features slick, smooth tires and a low-profile design that's built for outdoor or indoor play on hard surfaces like tile or hardwood.

This is because the remote control car is built for one thing and one thing only: drifting. Just like stunt drivers on a movie set, these cars spin and slide across the ground for cinematic turns and stylish maneuvering.

It has been revealed that bear in mind, however, that this car does not come ready to race. This is an assembly kit that requires patience, steady hands, and additional materials like glue and a hobby knife. Furthermore, the car will also require an electronic speed controller (ESC), battery, and radio receiver.

It has been revealed that if you aren't ready to commit to full-size model, this tiny RC car from Hot Wheels fits in the palm of your hand, and has an equally miniature price tag. While it doesn't have the speed or torque of the larger models on this list, this is a perfect way to introduce young kids to the thrill of remote control driving.

The mini Lambo, a 1/16th scale model, is also perfect gift for sports car lovers looking for a bit of fun. The RC car is built with a rechargeable battery already in the body. So, whenever it needs to be charged up, plug the cable directly into the car.

Recent findings suggest that the mini size is more for just convenience, too. The car is designed to fit and drive on all the same Hot Wheels tracks that work for the classic die cast models the brand is known for. So, if you already have a Hot Wheels enthusiast in mind, this is a great addition to their collection.

Based on our testing, the biggest distinction between RC cars is that some are hobby-grade models for racing or off-roading hobbyists, and others are beginner-friendly toys that are usually made for kids and beginners.

Sources indicate that hobby-grade RC cars come with powerful motors, beefy batteries, and the torque and speed to handle outdoor driving over tough terrain or competitive racing. These are typically more expensive than their toy counterparts and are better suited for buyers who want to seriously dive into RC cars or are already major fans. Toy RC cars are slower and get less run time per charge, but are much more affordable.

Sources indicate that RC cars also come in a wide variety of builds, including off-road 4x4s and buggies, rock crawlers (built for more rigid, extreme off-roading), and drift cars (best for turns and speed). You’ll often see the RC car’s scale listed, especially for model cars, representing its size in relation to the real deal.

While shopping, you may see the initials “RTR” in product descriptions, which stand for “ready to race.” This means you can start driving right out of the box or after charging, with no extra parts required to get it up and running. Cars may be labeled RTR even if the batteries are sold separately, though, so make sure to check the packaging.

Speed varies depending on what the car is built to do. For example, rock climbers don’t have to be incredibly fast to tackle boulders, but they need powerful high-torque motors, whereas a race car should hit at least 20 to 30 miles per hour, depending on your level of competition. Before you buy, make sure you have in mind where you expect most of your RC driving to happen and what kind of features are important to you.

If you want a taste of everything, there are a number of cars that are in the middle ground, offering enough speed to make straightaways fun and enough power to handle grass, inclines, and some gravel.

Less expensive RC cars generally have a two-button remote control, and those on the higher end have 2.4 GHz (a speedy signal transmission speed) pistol-grip-style remotes with more advanced steering and throttles. These remotes are more responsive, allowing you to make quick turns, rapidly accelerate, or even reverse at a moment's notice. 2.4 GHz remote controls are what you’ll likely see in any hobby-grade RC cars. If you go for a high-end model, ensure that replacement parts and upgrades are readily available. Otherwise, you’ll have to search for outdated parts on eBay.
