Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are at the moment scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen stated Sunday on CNN.

In a recent development, ​Van Hollen has also noted he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new problem is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

In a recent development, sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy remarked in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

Newly introduced member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

Industry observers note that that includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is presently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#100035. Tech Report: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (836 w)

Tech Report: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was currently looking at.
  • “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” claims the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy.
  • Recent findings suggest that it was unsettling, to say the least.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was currently looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

“Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” claims the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy. “That was one of the first things that I noticed,” he says. “And the cat even took on resemblances of people.”.

Recent findings suggest that it was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”.

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December glitch of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

The researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of major data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”.

It has been revealed that karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” states Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”.

Duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine notes. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

“What is newly introduced about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” claims Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”.

During a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine notes. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case indicates some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

According to recent reports, “It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl notes, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in newly introduced spots.

Recent findings suggest that using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom says. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”.

Sources indicate that we’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

This seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and notes it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

Sources indicate that the Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

The 8 Best Outdoor Security Cameras Keep an Eye on Your Home When You're Away

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark.
  • Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark. Installing a few security cameras around your property is an easy and surprisingly cost-effective way to level up your home security, adding watchful eyes that track comings and goings 24/7. Until relatively recently, the only options for personal home security were comprehensive (and expensive) systems that were installed and monitored by security professionals. Now, you can set up your own cameras and home security system that saves you cash without sacrificing performance.

Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins. According to Security.org, simply having a clearly visible camera or security device on your property serves as a strong deterrent for trespassers. Outdoor security cameras are equipped with features found in indoor security cameras like high-definition video, night vision, two-way audio, and more. In addition to this, they come equipped with outdoor-specific features like weather-resistant exteriors, sound detection, and integrated motion-activated spotlights.

It has been revealed that for this guide, we got our hands on the most promising options from well-established brands including Arlo, Wyze, Ring, and Eufy and tested them at our homes and offices. Read on below to learn about the best outdoor security cameras we recommend, along with expert advice to help you choose the right option for your home and budget.

It has been revealed that one quick note before we dive in: It’s increasingly important to pick security gear that’s compatible with whatever smart home system you already have. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV and has designed its products to more seamlessly connect with its other smart home devices. Same goes for Google products. If you already have a few items from a major smart home brand, consider buying gear that will be as compatible as possible with it.

More Home Improvement Stories: Best Retractable Awnings ● The Popular Mechanics 2025 Yard & Garden Awards ● Best Solar-Powered Outdoor Lights.

Industry observers note that we selected our recommendations based on a round of substantial testing: We installed these cameras outdoors, and used them to survey our homes for weeks, and in some cases months. We watched them as they watched our properties, as they endured a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

Recent findings suggest that we tested and compared their basic video recording functionality, evaluating them on clarity, field of view, and weather resistance as well as any special features they offer like spotlights, solar charging, sirens, and more. Some of the cameras on this list were tested in outdoor settings for months, facing a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We also tested their more nuanced security and tech features, including motion detection notifications, AI recognition of animals and packages, two-way audio conversations, and digital borders, among others. These features were considered as well as the cost, if any, associated with buying access to all of them.

We recommended the Wyze Outdoor Cam V2 ahead of testing, based on its low price, solid specs, and the past performance of other Wyze cameras that we've tested.

The Arlo Essential XL stands out for its user-friendly design, durable exterior, and of course, its clear video quality—all for a fair price. It's completely wireless, which means you can mount it anywhere around your home without worrying about power and wiring complications.

It excels as a 24/7 outdoor cam, with features like color night vision that improves the clarity of nighttime footage. During testing, we were impressed by its resolution in low light, as well as its accurate motion detection. It provides real-time alerts directly to your smartphone, and will let you check a live feed to observe any suspicious activity live as it happens.

Industry observers note that you can also program the integrated spotlight to automatically flash on when someone is within visual range. It's a great deterrent against potential robberies, and lets you leave the house without leaving a porch light on.

While this cam has solid features without a subscription, an Arlo Secure subscription adds cloud storage for your video footage, as well as additional target recognition and home security features, for $96 to $300 per year.

Arlo Essential XL Security Camera Review.

Few options balance price and quality as well as this affordable option from Wyze. The battery-operated Wyze Outdoor V2 camera can be mounted anywhere. Latest buyers should pick up the starter kit, which includes a base unit that allows you to expand your system with up to four cameras.

Though it's the most affordable on the list, it still offers a lineup of powerful features including motion-sensing technology that detects both body heat and movement, reducing the number of potential false alarms drastically.

The Wyze is also quite flexible for storage options with the camera capable of online cloud storage as well as localized storage on a microSD card.

Solar-powered cameras, while power-efficient, present extra setup challenges. Most of the time, the panel is attached to the body of the camera, so you need to need find to camera positions with a good field of view and get good sun exposure. Depending on the layout of your home and the surrounding area, that may lead to less-than-ideal placements, which create holes in your surveillance.

Sources indicate that the Tapo MagCam solves this concern with a detachable solar panel, so you can keep it connected when it's effective, or remove and mount it higher above the camera to get more sun. It features a 13-foot extension cord, so you have a good amount of slack to move it to an open, sunshiny space.

Test Editor Bradley Ford mounted his test camera in a semi-shaded area, then set up the solar panel in direct sunlight. Despite the fact that he was testing at the end of 2025, when there was significantly less daily sunlight, the battery never dipped below 80 percent charge. In the warmer weather, the camera typically sat at 100 percent.

In a recent development, in addition, Ford preferred that the MagCam relied on local storage. "One of the things we like best is that there is no need for a subscription to access activation videos," Ford stated. "They’re all stored locally on a Micro SD card in the camera. However, if you wish to pay for cloud storage, that option is also available.".

This specific kit comes with a camera, solar panel, and mount, however Tapo offers others with two or three cameras as well.

Our previous pick in this category, the Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Plus, was a terrific outdoor security camera that featured a dual-LED floodlight. The new Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro builds on that solid design with extra features, including support for dual-band WiFi and a “bird’s-eye view” feature that tracks a recorded subject as they move within the camera’s view, showing it on a top-down layout of the area.

The camera’s 1080p video resolution and 140-degree field of view are the same as the previous model, but image quality is enhanced with high dynamic range (HDR) support, which improves visibility in both low light and extremely bright conditions.

The lights themselves are also quite bright, 2000 lumens each, and the fixtures are adjustable so you can angle the light as you please.

It has been revealed that the Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro also features two-way audio support, with a 110-decibel siren that sounds when the system detects motion. It also offers customizable motion zones and 3D- motion radar for you to tailor to your property.

A word of warning: We found the wired installation was fairly difficult, so we recommend hiring an electrician unless you're experienced with wiring and up for a challenge.

It has been revealed that unlike any other outdoor security camera on our list, this option from Tactacam does not require a WiFi connection. Instead, it connects to cellular towers and works similarly to your smartphone. This makes the camera perfect for homes in remote locations.

The security camera does require a monthly subscription for access to on-demand videos and photos that are stored in the cloud, but looks start at just 5 bucks a month.

The device works with AA batteries or a rechargeable battery pack. In our testing, we took anywhere from two to 10 pictures a day and the pack lasted about three to four months before needing to be recharged.

In practice, the security camera is great at sensing motion more than 100 feet away, so it could potentially double as a nature cam. It lacks some of the features other, similarly priced models on this list have, but the biggest drawback is that the field of view is only about 50 feet wide.

The Arlo floodlight has everything we love from our top pick, including Arlo's superior app and software, but adds on a large floodlight, as well as a need for wired power.

Sources indicate that as with the Arlo Essential XL, you get quality motion detection software and color night vision. Spring for Arlo Secure, and you get AI target recognition that can point out passing cars or faces, and highlight packages.

Sources indicate that the floodlight also has some interesting features: Each light is individually adjustable, so you can angle them for the best possible coverage. That includes creative solutions like angling one light toward your back door, while pointing the other toward the steps leading to your back porch. It's a small touch, but a very appreciated one. It also includes a loud, 110-decibel siren.

If you're looking for a low-maintenance outdoor security camera system, eufy's S330 "eufycam 3" is a dynamic wireless option that supports solar charging and doesn't require professional installation.

Sources indicate that once installed and set up, we did not have to take either of the cameras down for recharging once over months of use. The solar panels kept them perpetually charged as long as they got exposure to a few hours of sunlight per day.

It has been revealed that it was similarly easy to connect the cameras to the greater home security. The outdoor cameras works through the home hub which after initial installation using an ethernet cable, works comfortably through your home WiFi. The cameras can then be set up anywhere within several hundred feet of the hub without losing connection.

A major benefit we also loved is the camera system requires no monthly subscription to access its features. This includes AI-powered face recognition, customizable activity zones, and of course, motion detection.

The only drawback for this camera set is the placement of the solar panels. While the panels being integrated directly on top of the camera makes it less cumbersome, it also means you need to install them in a spot with direct sunlight or they won't properly charge.

According to recent reports, the Reolink Argus 4 Pro gives you a sweeping 180-degree field of view, which allows you to cover large open spaces with as few cameras as possible. Properly positioned, you can achieve a near-complete view of an area with just two cameras.

In a recent development, this 4K camera features a dual-lens design that covers larger areas without blind spots or fishbowl-style warping. You'd think that might lead to complications with position or usage, but we found it easy to operate.

It features discrete solar panels for power, which allows for more placement flexibility: For example, you can install the camera under a ledge or rooftop, then secure the solar panel above, where it will get direct sun. That makes it easier to get the perfect shot and optimal power.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of storage, the Argus 4 Pro records footage locally and connects to a home hub. You don't have to pay a monthly fee for cloud storage or additional features. Simply turn it on, connect it the hub, and in theory, it should run without problem in perpetuity.

There are two types of consumer-grade home security cameras: wireless battery-powered cameras that you can set up easily nearly anywhere, but require you to occasionally replace batteries, and wired models that connect directly to your home's electrical system.

According to recent reports, wired cameras are generally more expensive and require an electrician's help unless you're comfortable with home wiring, but require far less maintenance once they're installed. Their placement is also restricted to locations where you can wired them in.

Recent findings suggest that battery-powered cameras, by contrast, are only restricted by the range of your WiFi router. Of course, you'll need to access them every few months to replace their batteries. Some models feature solar panels, giving you renewable energy, but panels also impose some placement restrictions. (Namely, access to sunlight).

Wired cameras do fall short of battery-powered models in one niche scenario—when the power goes out. Unlike, say, wired smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, which have reliable battery backup, you can't count on a wired security camera to provide surveillance footage during an extended period of time if there's a power failure. It varies from model to model, but most wired cameras can only last for 30 minutes to, at most, a few hours before they go dark.

It has been revealed that to avoid recording 24/7, which wastes power and storage space, outdoor security cameras usually feature motion sensors that trigger recording whenever there’s activity. Many cameras will also an alert to your companion app whenever they start recording.

According to recent reports, most cameras give you the ability to calibrate the motion sensor by setting motion zones in spots where you expect frequent false alarms, like a sidewalk. Others offer smart features that can differentiate between people, animals, and vehicles. You should also have the ability to customize your notifications, so you’ll only receive an alert in certain situations, like if it detects a person.

According to recent reports, furthermore, some cameras feature microphones, enabling audio detection, which can trigger recording and alerts based on nearby sounds that may be out of view (like a window breaking). Audio detection is a useful extra layer in a few specific situations, like when a single camera can’t cover the entire side of your home, but may also lead to more nuisance alerts. If you decide to use one, we recommend customizing your audio alert sensitivity if possible so you aren’t constantly getting notified when the neighbor’s dog barks.

The best outdoor security cameras record video in "Full HD" (1920 x 1080p) resolution, which captures enough detail to identify facial features or a car’s license plate. More expensive cameras record at higher resolutions, such as 2K or "Quad HD" (2560 x 1440p) or 4K Ultra HD (3840 x 2160) video, which deliver better detail. While higher resolution may help, 1080p video is usually clear enough to give you more than enough information in most situations.

Your camera’s field of view (FOV) is just as notable as its resolution. Field of view refers to how wide of an angle the lens is and therefore, how much of your yard or porch is in view. With a wider FOV, your camera can see a wider area around your property, providing more coverage. For the best results, we recommend a model with a field of view between 130 and 180 degrees.

According to recent reports, many outdoor cameras also feature an integrated spotlight that can illuminate the surroundings if motion is detected, improving visibility in low-light situations. A spotlight also acts as a deterrent by making potential intruders more visible. Similarly, the majority of outdoor cameras offer some kind of night vision feature, which uses infrared (IR) lights to record a high-contrast black and white video in the dark. Top-of-the-line cameras are capable of recording standard video in low light, minimizing the need for night vision.

There’s no point in recording camera footage if you can’t store it for when you need it. Many manufacturers offer free cloud storage for a limited time—typically seven days–after which video is overwritten with fresh recordings. You can always download and save that footage, so long as you do during that initial window.

Sources indicate that if you want to save your footage for a longer period, there are a couple of options. Many companies provide additional cloud storage for a subscription fee. There are also cameras that feature a microSD card slot for storing footage locally. This does require a bit of extra maintenance in the form of occasionally removing the card and either deleting or downloading the recorded data to free up more space on the card.

If you’re concerned with privacy, be aware that cloud footage is generally kept on a manufacturer’s servers, which can be stolen if the manufacturer’s digital security is breached. Some companies may also use or share data from stored recordings in ways you might not anticipate. For example, Amazon has shared footage from Ring cameras to law enforcement without customers’ permission on many occasions. While storing locally requires more legwork, it is definitely the most secure option for privacy-conscious homeowners.

According to recent reports, security cameras are more than just their features. Nearly all security cameras are built to connect with other smart home devices. So, before buying any specific option, make sure it is compatible with the devices you already own. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV. There are many brands that work with the majority of the smart home software available such as Apple, Google Nest, and Ring. Some have limited functionality on other smart home software systems outside of their brand, but still work with them. Furthermore, most security camera brands require a monthly subscription to gain full access to many of their features. These monthly subscriptions range in price and overall necessity with some basically essential to operate the cameras and store footage in the cloud while others are designed as a bonus add-on to the base product. Prior to purchase, make sure to take a close look at both the smart home compatibility as well as what comes with and without the monthly subscription service.

Most of the outdoor security cameras we recommend are sold individually or as part of a larger set. The number of cameras you need for your property will vary, based on your home security plan and how much camera coverage you want. A well-installed camera with a wide field of view can cover an important and vulnerable area on your property, such as a back door or garage.

According to recent reports, that remarked, even a small home will need at least a few cameras to achieve full coverage on every ground-level door and window. You may need multiple cameras to reveal tricky blind spots created by corners, lawn features, and anything else that might impede a single camera position.

Don't freak out about needing a fleet of surveillance gear, though. Not everyone wants or needs to have every single square inch of their property under constant watch. It’s up to you to decide where you want an extra eye. The vital thing is to make sure you know what you need before making a purchase.

Of course. There are no features of an outdoor security camera that would prevent it from working inside. That said, many companies make indoor cameras that are cheaper, and may feature a stand or mounting options that make more sense for blending in with your home or office.

You should always be careful when considering home security. Over the years, there have been multiple reports of strangers accessing live video feeds and recorded videos from home security cameras.

Luckily, there are simple ways to protect yourself. As with other devices, adhering to digital security best practices, such as keeping your smart home devices’ firmware up to date, creating a strong password and activating two-factor authentication wherever possible, will help prevent a breach.

Industry observers note that you may also have concerns about who has access to video that’s stored in the cloud. Most companies ask for permission to review recordings for research and development purposes. Depending on the tech giant, this request often comes in the form of an “opt-in” setting in the camera app, though some may turn it on by default unless you “opt out.”.

Some may also share recordings with law enforcement. In some cases, they will only do so when compelled by a search warrant. A couple manufacturers, specifically Amazon (Ring) and Google (Nest), have remarked they will provide footage without a warrant if law enforcement claims it is an emergency.

#100031. Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (386 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders.
  • Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
  • Recent findings suggest that paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.

Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.

Recent findings suggest that paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.“I was genuinely amazed,” states Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”.

Under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.

The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the new family Hydrelcanidae.

Industry observers note that “Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu notes. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.

The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.

And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team notes.

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden stated he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s latest book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major complications of our time.

According to recent reports, it’s often mentioned that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

Industry observers note that the sheer length of his upcoming book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single concern in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he indicates. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

It has been revealed that one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

Sources indicate that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

In a recent development, describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden indicates. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have remarked it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

Industry observers note that “I had it on good authority that several massive names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

I’ve spent years testing vacuums for Popular Mechanics, and that experience informs a lot of my recommendations below. Some of these models have been through my own series of hands-on tests, while others made the cut based on my familiarity with their brands and product lines, along with research into their features and real-world performance. According to recent reports, the Shark PowerDetect is a feature-packed option for anyone who wants a cordless stick vacuum that does a lot of the thinking for them. In a recent development, the hinged wand is great for cleaning under furniture and makes it a lot easier to reach hidden areas without having to bend down at all kinds of weird angles. It’s on the heavier side, and the long recharge time is a drawback, but strong pickup and smart features make it a good pick for whole-home cleaning.

Recent findings suggest that don’t let the price fool you: The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder is a strong and versatile cordless vacuum. It isn’t too heavy to carry between rooms, and the self-standing design means you don’t have to remount it or lay it flat any time you need to pause during your cleaning session.

It has been revealed that it has a tangle-free brush roll that does a great job picking up pet hair (as well as your own stray strands around the house). I also like the LED headlights that show hidden dirt, dust, and debris on floors and furniture. The attachments are great for above-floor cleaning, too. Battery life drops considerably when you crank up the suction power, so it’s best for maintenance cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Review.

The LVAC-300 packs cleaning power and everyday convenience into a lightweight machine. According to recent reports, it converts to a handheld vacuum cleaner with attachments for upholstery, stairs, and car interiors, and it uses a pleated mechanical HEPA filter with a dense arrangement of fibers to capture even the tiniest dust particles. It has been revealed that I like that this model uses HEPA filtration to capture up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and odors (which is great if you’re a pet owner). Marella Cruises‘ Discovery 2 is currently undergoing enhancements in a wet dock in Málaga, Spain.

According to a recent social media update, the 1995-built vessel is being prepared to become an adults-only vessel, in addition to undergoing routine maintenance.

The former Legend of the Seas will undergo engine work and main pool retiling, with the Glass House Pool getting a fresh coat of paint and the atrium new seating, complete with a refreshed Snack Shack.

The ship is set to welcome only adults starting in 2027 with former youth facilities transformed into four fresh venues, including Marella’s first private karaoke lounge.

Amplify Karaoke will operate as a private lounge for up to seven guests, which can be booked by the hour.

Other newly introduced venues include the Lost Luggage Bureau, a speakeasy venue inspired by the Golden Age of Travel, allowing passengers to take part in two 90-minute shows that include live music, live actors, storytelling and three signature cocktails.

The Marella Discovery 2 will also introduce Red Handed, an escape room set backstage at the fictional Cabaret Rouge in the 1920s, where teams of up to six guests have 60 minutes to steal Lady Ruby Bardot’s diamond necklace before they’re caught red-handed.

Also being added is The Loft, which is described as a calm space for passengers who want to slow down, combining a library, board games, and hosted arts and crafts in a relaxed setting.

Following the enhancements in wet dock, the Marella Discovery 2 is scheduled to operate a winter season in the Canaries and Madeira, offering seven-night cruises from Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Puerto del Rosario to destinations in Spain and Portugal.

#100016. Breaking: A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio.
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • On the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 new safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

On the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

Engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

According to recent reports, as the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted swiftly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

Sources indicate that the train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

Industry observers note that faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

Recent findings suggest that in the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

Sources indicate that in the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

According to recent reports, some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

Even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”.

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace noted. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”.

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

According to recent reports, with the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

From the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

In a recent development, after consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid firm were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

The agency published the first investigation revision to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

The first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly demonstrated flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he said. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he said. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

Recent findings suggest that the other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

In a recent development, east Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she noted. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”.

According to recent reports, wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern unveiled that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the firm nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a recent development, in a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick mentioned. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”.

Recent findings suggest that the roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

The place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical issues.

Recent findings suggest that in March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”.

Recent findings suggest that this October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a upcoming layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Recent findings suggest that following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

The most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the initiative in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

For a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these major Shamu tanks,” Wallace said. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

Recent findings suggest that however, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

A-Rosa has entered a strategic partnership with Columbia blue to strengthen crew management and onboard hotel services across the European river cruise fleet.

Starting at the beginning of 2027, the Columbia signature brand will take responsibility for selected hotel crew recruitment administration and operational hotel services across the A-Rosa fleet operating on the Rhine, Danube, Rhône and Seine rivers.

The collaboration is designed to strengthen operational stability, broaden access to qualified personnel and support the long-term growth ambitions of A-Rosa, according to a press release.

Recent findings suggest that rolf-Dieter Maltzahn, CEO of A-Rosa, said: “With Columbia blue, we are combining the brand and product expertise of A-Rosa with international recruitment and hospitality expertise. In this way, we are strengthening the continuous ability to offer our future guests the quality and personal travel experience that A-Rosa stands for.”.

Under the agreement, A-Rosa will retain its vertically integrated business model, including its own tour operator, shipping manufacturer and fleet, maintaining full responsibility for strategic direction, brand positioning, product development, quality standards and the guest experience.

Columbia blue will complement this by providing specialist operational services, with A-Rosa remaining the framework for all onboard hotel operations.

Recent findings suggest that “A-Rosa has a strong brand, a distinct product promise and extensive experience in the European river cruise market. We look forward to contributing our expertise and working together to develop an efficient and resilient model for hotel services,’’ noted Norman Schmiedl, CEO of Columbia blue.

The agreement comes as the increase in capacity, fresh market entrants and intensifying competition for experienced hospitality professionals across the European river cruise sector place greater demands on operators to secure skilled personnel.

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, declared Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

In a recent development, his announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Recent findings suggest that evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

Industry observers note that “Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign remarked in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”.

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie mentioned in a statement.
