Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

📅 23 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006.
  • There was much to do here but that was the point.
  • It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

Industry observers note that if you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Industry observers note that tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

Recent findings suggest that but as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”.

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”.

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It has been revealed that it pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Because your choices do have an impact.

Recent findings suggest that riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got significant because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#99976. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1566 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nomadicmatt ↗ Open Full Page

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that drones are huge.
  • There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

Recent findings suggest that what make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

Sources indicate that the sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

In a recent development, most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

Recent findings suggest that the Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

Recent findings suggest that the drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

Here’s a video of the drone in action:.

According to recent reports, the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

According to recent reports, the color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

According to recent reports, while 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

Industry observers note that the Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

In a recent development, while the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#99975. How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1596 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive.
  • Sources indicate that you could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

According to recent reports, I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

Sources indicate that you could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

Historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

From the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

Sources indicate that after a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

Back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

It has been revealed that close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

Day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

It has been revealed that the delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

Or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

Recent findings suggest that A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

Industry observers note that naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

Recent findings suggest that for a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road.
  • Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).
  • Industry observers note that but, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

Industry observers note that but, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

It has been revealed that they started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

At the moment, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in latest destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Recent findings suggest that outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Recent findings suggest that every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Sources indicate that plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

Sources indicate that and the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!).

It has been revealed that plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

In a recent development, at Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That noted, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Industry observers note that second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you initiative on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Sources indicate that is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

According to recent reports, is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy complications).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing newly introduced cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

It has been revealed that outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

“I stated, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.
  • Sources indicate that the carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027.
  • American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

Sources indicate that the carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

Recent findings suggest that israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and Latest York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

American also mentioned Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava noted in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Latest York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

#99970. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2452 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nomadicmatt ↗ Open Full Page

Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city.
  • Industry observers note that like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow.
  • I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Industry observers note that like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

It has been revealed that being such a major city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you strategy an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

Recent findings suggest that this first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

Sources indicate that after a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

According to recent reports, nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Recent findings suggest that madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

Sources indicate that one popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Sources indicate that another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

Industry observers note that on your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

According to recent reports, the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial mentioned to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

It has been revealed that while Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

The Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027?
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of newly introduced flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root.
  • Recent findings suggest that from untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a substantial birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027? No wonder: 2026 was a bumper year for European travel, from the Winter Olympics fueling a surging obsession with the Dolomites to the total solar eclipse bringing hoards of umbraphiles to the Balearic Islands, and celebrity weddings adding to an ever-growing love for Sicily. But as we edge closer to the end of the year, there are a few clear-cut destinations we’re most looking forward to visiting (and recommending to you, our fellow travelers) for the 12 months to come.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of newly introduced flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root. These nominations make up the Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027—and we promise they are worthy of your precious vacation time and hard-earned spending money.

Recent findings suggest that from untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a substantial birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027. Happy travels. —Olivia Morelli.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: untamed wilderness and peaceful pockets.

The Albanian Alp's village of Theth is a patch of pastoral living—and fantastic hiking trails.

Local bed-and-breakfasts and guesthouses welcome trekkers, who do both day treks and through hikes connecting small towns.

Industry observers note that as Albania’s allure continues to grow, travelers flock to the Adriatic beaches of the south. But in the northern alpine region, the scenery offers a different type of drama—jagged snow-dipped peaks, turquoise rivers, hut-to-hut hiking—and in place of shiny seaside hotels, Albanian-owned wooden B&Bs welcome alpinists for home-cooked meals after long, satisfying days on the many surrounding trails. This area was largely isolated during the communist era, given its strategic location along the borders with Montenegro and Kosovo, which means that it has been slower to open its arms to the world (that’s also why you’ll stumble into countless abandoned bunkers from this period on your hike). The feeling here is that you can still show up to a guesthouse without a reservation, you can still camp wherever you find a spot, and, yet, there is also the sense that if you aren’t seeing this place now, or within the next couple years, you’ll miss the precious moment when it still feels like a secret to be let in on.

Recent findings suggest that start your trip in the charming city of Shköder, known as the gateway to the Alps, where bikepackers cycle through the city, and restaurant patios spill over with guests enjoying glasses of Albanian wine. From there, many travelers blueprint stops in the villages of Theth and Valbona (a stunningly scenic one-day through-hike links the two of them), or embark on ambitious multi-day journeys on routes like the Peak of the Balkans, which traces a two-week-long loop crossing into Kosovo and Montenegro. Infrastructure improvements have made roads and trails to access this region better in recent years, with much more where that came from. What was once only known by residents and those who purchased their paper guides now exists online, meaning it is also possible to base yourself in, say, the Eden-like Valbona Valley, and embark on a latest route each day. Increasingly, there are elevated places to stay that preserve the soul of this place, opening in a slow trickle like Valbona Resort and Spa (2024) and SeSam Villas in Theth (2025). There may be folklore calling these the Accursed Mountains, but only because they are so vast and dramatic that their geography has historically kept intruders out. For hikers, that means a literal playground, with Albanian hosts leading the way. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: the next World Expo centered on play, and a booming hotel scene to match.

Belgrade is set to host the World Expo in summer 2027, and a flock of upcoming hotels will be ready to receive the travelers it is sure to bring.

Recent findings suggest that all the world’s coming to Belgrade next year—and, it seems, coming to play. The Balkan city will host the next edition of the World Expo, a spiritual successor to the World Fair where nations come to exchange their latest and greatest cultural achievements and boldest ideas for the future. From May 15 to August 15, 2027, Belgrade plans to welcome over four million visitors to explore the theme of “Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All." Its status as a host city feels especially symbolic as the Balkans emerge as a leader in technology and innovation across Europe. To meet the occasion, the city’s hotel scene is stepping up, with 15 new openings slated to cut the ribbon by the time the program kicks off. The crown jewel in the portfolio is the Ritz-Carlton, Belgrade, which will occupy a prime spot on the Danube riverfront. Other major names to watch out for include the InterContinental Belgrade and the Swissôtel Belgrade. In total, these projects will add roughly 1,500 to 2,000 new hotel rooms to the city. The shiny, new threads go well with the old in a place as historic as the Serbian capital, which lays claim to grand sites such as the Church of St. Sava, one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world, and the Museum of Yugoslavia, which has a sprawling eight-acre park complex. —Kat Chen.

Go for: a coveted summer destination at its sweet spot.

A slew of luxury openings like Aman and Mandarin Oriental have arrived in Bodrum over the past few years, with NG Sign Bodrum and Bvlgari on the horizon.

Industry observers note that for the past few summers, the glittering Bodrum peninsula has welcomed a wave of luxury openings, transforming this once-sleepy harbor town into one of the Aegean's most coveted corners. Aman, Mandarin Oriental, and homegrown Maçakizi were early champions of the scene and remain firmly at the heart of its appeal, but a new generation of hotels, restaurants, and beach clubs has since made Bodrum one of Europe’s most sought-after summer escapes.

Recent findings suggest that mayfair and Knightsbridge restaurant favorites Zuma, Bagatelle, and Novikov have all made the journey east in recent years, accompanied in 2026 by oh-so-chic arrivals from Dubai, Paris, and Marbella (Gaia, Gigi Rigolatto, and Maison Revka). Together they have helped recast Bodrum as a playground for the international jet set, bringing with them a distinctly cosmopolitan, see-and-be-seen energy.

This summer also brought the long-awaited arrival of the adults-only hideaway Oku, the latest in the brand's collection of design-led retreats in Ibiza, Kos, and Andalusia. Throw in annual beach-club takeovers from the likes of Jacquemus and Alo, as well as boutique openings by brands like Cartier, and it seems there’s barely a name in luxury that isn’t lining up to plant its flag here.

But 2027 promises to be the sweet spot. With fewer headline-grabbing launches, the peninsula settles into a quieter rhythm, and openings such as Yahşi Bay’s NG Sign Bodrum, a villa hotel of sun-filled, glass-walled residences with two to six bedrooms, put privacy ahead of spectacle. It's the summer to explore Bodrum at its most relaxed. Reservations are likely to be easier to come by as last year’s hottest tables settle in for the upcoming season and the eyes of trend followers will be trained elsewhere, leaving the regulars to do what they’ve always done: Dance as the sun sets on the wooden deck of Maçakizi, wander the meyhane-lined promenade of fishing village Gümüşlük, stopping for fresh seafood as they go; or hop between the coastline’s secluded bays, tucking into late-afternoon picnics beneath the pine trees.

Recent findings suggest that enjoy it while it lasts. In 2028, all eyes will return to the peninsula as Bvlgari opens its sprawling hillside resort above yacht-speckled Paradise Bay, giving Europe's luxury travel crowd fresh reason to return. —Sophie Prideaux.

Go for: Irish hospitality and spectacular sporting scenes.

The 46th Ryder Cup will take place at Adare Manor in County Limerick.

Designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio, Adare is nestled upon 840 acres of parkland.

Home to natural wonders, ancient castles, lively pubs, and famously friendly locals, Ireland has long captivated travelers. While the well-trodden tourist trail takes in perennial favorites, 2027 will see another destination step into the spotlight. County Limerick, on the west coast, is gearing up to host one of the world’s greatest sporting events: the 46th Ryder Cup. Between September 17 and 19, the tournament will take place on the pristine fairways of the prestigious golfing estate Adare Manor. Designed by renowned golf course architect Tom Fazio, the championship course is set within 840 acres of magnificent parkland surrounding the estate’s 19th-century Neo-Gothic castle—a fairytale destination worth visiting at any time of year.

Beyond golf, Limerick has a rich sporting heritage. Thomond Park, home of Munster Rugby, is one of the best-supported grounds in the world, with match days bringing a buzz to the city. Beyond the sporting calendar, there’s plenty to discover. Highlights include the 13th-century King John’s Castle, the Hunt Museum for its art collection including works by Picasso and Renoir, and Lough Gur, an idyllic lake beside Ireland’s oldest and largest stone circle. Limerick also makes an excellent base for exploring the Wild Atlantic Way. Around an hour northwest of the city, Lahinch is widely regarded as one of Ireland’s best surf beaches, while the spectacular Cliffs of Moher rank among the country’s most beloved landmarks. With world-class golf, a proud sporting heritage, fascinating history, and easy access to some of Ireland’s most spectacular scenery, Limerick is set to have its moment in 2027. —Camilla Hewitt.

Go for: a city break that’ll stay with you long after you’ve left.

In Cologne's Old Town, the charm is in the details, like this whale lantern outside Brauhaus Sünner im Walfisch .

If you visit for Cologne's exuberant carnival, say as the locals say: “Morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“Tomorrow is what you make of it!”).

Let’s be honest: Cologne doesn’t necessarily win you over at first sight. It is not a conventionally beautiful city; rather, it is a feeling. Even locals will tell you that the city gets under your skin. Anyone who has experienced Cologne’s exuberant carnival spilling onto its streets and into its clubs and pubs is likely to fall for the city—and its people—for good. The motto for the so-called fifth season in 2027 is “morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“tomorrow is what you make of it!”). Multiple crises or not, the people of Cologne refuse to let anything dampen their spirits.

According to recent reports, and while folk culture is a major part of Cologne’s appeal, the city’s high culture is equally compelling. In September 2026, the opera house on Offenbachplatz finally reopened after 15 years of renovation—an occasion eagerly anticipated by many. Just 160 yards away is Kolumba, the museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Peter Zumthor. Its lofty, lime-washed rooms and the gentle light filtering through the narrow gaps between walls and floor provide a quietly dramatic setting for the art—and a welcome respite from the bustle of the city. Zumthor built the museum around the ruins of the former St. Kolumba church, incorporating the Madonna in the Ruins chapel by Gottfried Böhm. The work of two exceptional architects brought together in one place: that alone is reason enough to come.

The Museum Ludwig is another perennial draw. In 2026, it recorded its highest-ever visitor numbers thanks to its exhibition devoted to the late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. Art, in Cologne, is very much a capital-A affair. Every autumn, the international art world descends on the city for Art Cologne, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair, which celebrates its 60th anniversary in 2027. The 200th anniversary of Beethoven’s death is being marked in equally spectacular fashion. Throughout the year, the Cologne Symphony Orchestra will welcome a stellar line-up of renowned conductors and ensembles. The musical celebrations culminate in October, when pianist Igor Levit will take on all 32 of the great composer’s piano sonatas in a single evening.

According to recent reports, the city’s famously warm and open-hearted inhabitants are just as welcoming when it comes to gastronomic newcomers. Julia Komp, who became Germany’s youngest Michelin-starred chef in 2016 at the age of 27, knows this well. Today, her restaurant Sahila is firmly at the forefront of Cologne’s culinary scene. Other top tables include the intimate 20-seat Onda on Händelstrasse; Vunky on Eigelstein, specializing in plant-based fine dining; Toki, the city’s first kaiseki restaurant; and the recently opened Kluth, whose six-course surprise menu, “et kütt wie et kütt” (“it is what it is”), takes its name from a quintessential Cologne saying. —Ilona Marx.

Go for: rugged landscapes and cinematic coastlines.

Sailing yacht Orient Express Corinthian's itineraries will set sail to Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent in 2027.

Hotel Basgi Basgi is a favorite among design lovers in Corsica—a grow that is increasingly looking to the island.

When Simon Jacquemus chose Phare de la Pietra, a 19th-century lighthouse on a rocky Corsican peninsula, as the backdrop for his Spring 2027 fashion show this summer, it was easy to see why. The designer, long inspired by the interplay of place, light, and raw emotion, described his show Le Bonheur (meaning “happiness” or “bliss”) as “a cliff that I add colors on top. An impressionist painting.”.

It's true. Corsica is a place where cinematic elegance meets rugged natural beauty. It's why the island was once named Kallisté, meaning “most beautiful,” by the ancient Greeks. Here, dramatic mountains meet wild hinterlands and fiery red rockfaces jut against turquoise waters, making for breathtaking hiking through UNESCO-listed landscapes such as the Scandola Nature Reserve.

The island long slipped under the radar compared with neighboring Sardinia and the French Riviera. But Jacquemus’ arrival, coupled with a flurry of recent smart hotel openings, suggests that may not be the case for much longer. Leading the charge is A Mandria di Murtoli, a 10-room retreat spread across five restored stone buildings in the Ortolo Valley, which is a little sister to epicurean Domaine de Murtoli, where farm-to-table living is the order of the day. Elsewhere, Hotel Mylos on the west coast and Basgi Basgi in the north are drawing an increasingly design-conscious crowd.

According to recent reports, adding to the island’s momentum is the maiden voyage of the Orient Express Corinthian, a sailing yacht with 2027 itineraries calling at Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent, opening up Corsica's fishing ports, medieval citadels, and spectacular coastline to a newly introduced wave of travelers. —Ashleigh Spiliopoulou.

Go for: a coolcation destination with Michelin status.

Newly-opened Betty Beach brings street food and brewery offerings to the beachfront of the Danish Riviera.

The 60-mile so-called Danish Rivera is dotted with fishing villages, seaside resorts, and beaches.

Recent findings suggest that with rising summer temperatures across Europe, the Danish Riviera has emerged as the continent's favorite coastal coolcation destination. This 60-mile coastal stretch in Northern Zealand brings travelers the aesthetic appeal and culinary credibility of Copenhagen, but in a relaxed setting of fishing villages, sandy beaches, forests, and historical seaside resorts that remain largely undiscovered by international visitors.

It has been revealed that the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Humlebæk marks the southern end of the riviera, but many visitors staying in Copenhagen don't venture any further north to seaside towns. Many of the region's charming seaside hotels date back to the late 19th century. But a fresh generation of stays is rejuvenating the landscape with contemporary design. Cori in Hornbæk brings barefoot energy to a beautifully repurposed former hospital, and Hôtel de Ville in Gilleleje transforms an old town hall into an eclectic boutique spa hotel.

Exceptional gastronomy abounds, with Michelin-starred standouts such as Jordnær, The Samuel, and Parsley Salon representing New Nordic Cuisine at its finest. For something more casual, recently opened Betty Beach combines beachfront dining, street food, and a brewery for sun-kissed imbibing. Denmark's first official wine route rolled out last year in North Zealand and Odsherred, with nine wineries offering tours and tastings of cold-climate grape varietals such as Solaris and Rondo. —Amber Gibson.

Go for: wild Austen-esque adventures and spa stays galore.

Dartmoor's vast landscape, made of granite tors, walking paths, and moorland, brings the drama of Sense and Sensibility to life.

It has been revealed that dartmoor has always lent itself to drama. Wild ponies pick their way through heather, granite tors loom out of the mist, and the ever-changing weather plays a starring role. Now it’s getting its close-up as the backdrop of Georgia Oakley’s newly introduced Sense and Sensibility adaptation in theaters in September 2026. The film was shot around Princetown, Tavistock, and Gutter Tor, and its release coincides with Dartmoor National Park’s 75th anniversary. As the Austen connection pulls focus to Dartmoor, 2027 is the year to stay a little longer and explore a little further.

It’s unusually special in the depths of winter, when the weather gets wild. Picture misty mornings walking the ancient tracks and climbing tors, and afternoons yomping across moorland in conditions that demand retreating somewhere cozy for a hot bath and a roaring fire. For a hands-on experience, book one of the free conservation days running on selected Sundays in 2027 to learn more about Dartmoor’s prehistoric archaeology, wildlife, and rare species while helping to preserve its future. Don’t miss Tavistock, the old market town on Dartmoor’s western edge. Its handsome Pannier Market is bursting with antiques and curiosities, ideal for a spot of treasure hunting. For a change of pace, visit 11th-century Buckfast Abbey, where the Benedictine monks still make their famous tonic wine to a secret recipe.

According to recent reports, to feel like a main character in your own period drama, book a room at Boringdon Hall. This show-stopping historical hotel on the edge of the moor combines roaring fires and old-world grandeur with one of Devon’s best spas. Its Michelin-starred Àclèaf restaurant retained its star in 2026, a quietly heroic achievement in a world obsessed with shiny newly introduced openings. There is nothing like spending the wildest part of the year getting wind-beaten on Dartmoor, then retreating for a spa treatment, proper grub, and a fire. —Zoe Cook.

Go for: a hidden culture hotspot on the Iberian Peninsula.

Évora, Portugal's prettiest city, is now home to the Vermelho by Christian Louboutin hotel.

Évora's artisan traditions that helped earn the city its title as a European Capital of Culture.

It has been revealed that although there’s really no need to do so—Évora is impressive in its own right—we sometimes refer to this little historic city as the Seville of Portugal. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986, its center comprises an imposing Roman temple, known as the Temple of Diana; a Gothic cathedral; the eerie Baroque Cathedral of Bones, next to the Church of St. Francis; and the Renaissance Palace of King Manuel I.

Industry observers note that in 2027, Évora will turn even more heads as one of the European Capitals of Culture. But Portugal’s prettiest city remains, overwhelmingly, a peaceful place, where at many times of the year you can stroll around in near silence. Then there’s the food. Restaurants such as Tua Madre, A Cozinha do Paço, and Forno da Telha allow you to discover recipes deeply rooted in the land and tradition. Don’t leave without trying porco à alentejana (clams and pork stew), ensopado de borrego (lamb stew), and a variety of local soups. And bread—plenty of bread—with superb olive oil. There’s also wine, of course, produced on the herdades (traditional estates dotted throughout the Alentejo region). After so much eating, you’ll need to get out and about. Which is perhaps why we find the concept behind Évora’s status as a European Capital of Culture so charming—the motto is based on the Alentejo’s cultural way of being: vagar, or to wander. —David Moralejo.

Fuerteventura's volcanic landscape offers a stirring contrast to its surf beaches—and a unique draw for travelers headed to the Canary Islands.

Boutique stay Casa Montelongo is one of several design-forward gems, this one tucked away in the charming village of La Oliva.

The second-largest and oldest of the Canary Islands, Fuerteventura is quickly establishing itself as one of the archipelago’s leading destinations. First came Paradisus by Meliá Fuerteventura, followed more recently by Zel Fuerteventura (the lifestyle brand created by Rafael Nadal in partnership with Meliá Hotels International). Set side by side, the two resorts form the Atlantic’s first wellness hub, set within a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Their privileged location on Sotavento beach completes the experience, with stretches of white sand and crystal-clear waters synonymous with the island.

Fuerteventura is also recognized as one of the world's best destinations for water sports, particularly windsurfing and kitesurfing. The area surrounding both hotels is home to René Egli by Meliá, a renowned water sports center. And beyond its coastline, the island continues to stand out. Charming villages such as La Oliva are home to a upcoming generation of boutique projects, including Casa Montelongo, one of the area's hidden gems. With the spectacular Corralejo Dunes, traditional Majorero cheese, and dramatic volcanic and desert landscapes contrasting with idyllic beaches, Fuerteventura is emerging as the ideal destination for travelers seeking a holiday centered on sport, wellness, relaxation, and reconnection. —Maria Ángeles Cano.

Go for: a vibrant city finally getting its moment in the spotlight.

Beyond Liepāja's beaches, converted historic and Soviet-era buildings are a reason to visit this cultural hub in 2027.

Sources indicate that plenty of the most seasoned travelers have never heard of Liepāja. That’s about to change: the Baltic coastal city has been named a European Capital of Culture in 2027, bringing a year-long program of public art, performances, and festivals with an allocated $11 million in funding. Curious visitors casting their gaze towards the little-known city will discover art-nouveau architecture, an atmospheric former naval district, and one of the longest urban beaches in Northern Europe.

Sources indicate that it’s certainly smaller and considerably less visited than Riga, but the repurposed historic and Soviet-era spaces are strangely wonderful. Wiktorija, a former cinema dating from 1913, now operates as a multi-use cultural venue hosting everything from poetry evenings to rock concerts. Take a guided tour around Karosta, the former Tsarist and Soviet naval district, to explore the history of landmarks like the striking St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral. The Great Amber Concert Hall, meanwhile, is home to the Liepāja Symphony Orchestra, the oldest in the Baltics, which is already expanding its program ahead of 2027. Rooted firmly in the present rather than the Soviet past are businesses like MO Liepāja in Julianna's Courtyard, a cluster of restored industrial buildings along the Trade Canal now housing restaurants, bars, and creative outposts such as local surfboard maker Drtyboards. —Amber Gibson.

Go for: a charm-packed city break, with newly introduced hotels and gorgeous coastal scenes to boot.

Naples will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup next summer.

According to recent reports, as for where to rest your head? Rocco Forte Hotels will open a 46-suite stay in the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano.

It has been revealed that gritty and pretty, chaotic and cultured, ancient and contemporary, Naples is one of Italy's most exhilarating cities. In 2027, the Campanian capital will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup (July 10 to 18), an event that has accelerated the regeneration of the industrial Bagnoli waterfront. Away from the waves, the hospitality scene is evolving, too. Rocco Forte Hotels will open its first Naples property, a 46-suite retreat occupying the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano, restored by architect Michele Bönan, and complete with a rooftop pool looking out over the Bay of Naples and Mount Vesuvius.

According to recent reports, but Naples has never needed another reason to visit, with masterpieces such as Caravaggio's The Seven Works of Mercy and Giuseppe Sanmartino's Veiled Christ, and the antiquities of its National Archaeological Museum, whose forthcoming second site, Mann II, will bring thousands of artifacts out of storage. The city’s contemporary art scene continues to evolve at the Madre Museum, which recently welcomed internationally acclaimed curator Eugenio Viola as its new director. Nearby, Pompeii and Herculaneum agricultural parks remain as compelling as ever. And then, of course, there’s the warmth and spirit of the Neapolitan people.

Da Attilio, Concettina ai Tre Santi, 50 Kalò, Diego Vitagliano, and Pizzaria La Notizia are practically compulsory for pizza, but there’s more to the city’s rich food scene. Donna Teresa and Mimì alla Ferrovia are among the beloved mainstays serving some of the finest traditional Neapolitan cuisine. —Jaclyn de Giorgio.

Go for: an under-the-radar Ionian gem.

According to recent reports, parga is the kind of Grecian destination every traveler hopes to find: easy to reach, yet seemingly under the radar. Upcoming hotels in 2026 and 2027 add to the appeal, without blowing its cover.

Glittering Ionian water, pine-clad hills tumbling into a colorful harbor, and a Venetian castle above it all: Parga is undoubtedly picturesque. Yet this little corner of the Greek mainland remains surprisingly under the radar. Its old town is made for slow wandering, leisurely lunching on seafood or traditional Greek mezze at waterfront tavernas, and exploring seriously beautiful beaches such as Valtos, a gold sand bay with award-winning Blue Flag credentials. Inland, meanwhile, the Acheron River makes a heavenly setting for horseback riding, rafting, canyon walks, and swimming.

Part of Parga’s appeal is how easy it is to reach: Tiny-but-mighty Preveza Airport is only an hour away, making this feel like a secret without the schlep. Parga Beach Resort, directly on Valtos Beach, makes a particularly excellent base. Its upcoming beachfront suites, launched in late summer 2026, sleep up to two adults and four children. A regular water taxi nips around the bay to Parga town, turning supper in that spectacular harbor into part of the adventure. The 2027 opening of Varko Bay nearby will add another high-end stay, with villas, a spa, sandy beaches, and a private marina. —Zoe Cook.
