📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

Sources indicate that I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”.

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!).

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that released coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty latest to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

It’s available in all 50 states.

Faye has one strategy for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of intends and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:.

In a recent development, these limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:.

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a firm allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:.

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

According to recent reports, telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!).

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!).

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a upcoming outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

Sources indicate that for larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

It has been revealed that the combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#99967. 16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary

16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task.
  • Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030.
  • Sources indicate that perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task. Whether you’re looking for a charming riad stay in Marrakech, yearn for serenity and seclusion in the Atlas Mountains or strategy to immerse yourself in the Agafay desert, there’s so more to this colorful country than the promise of winter sun. It’s perhaps obvious, then, why Morocco has long since been favored by the fashionable jet set crowd, and has become home to so many notable hotel addresses. Some are so lavish they veer on palaces, others are romantically reimagined farmhouses or bohemian beachside boltholes.

Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030. One of the biggest changes is the multi-million dollar rail expansion project, which will connect Kenitra with Marrakech, via Rabat and Casablanca. On the hotel front, Four Seasons is set to open a upcoming address in Tangier, while Virgin Limited Edition intends to open a hotel near Marrakech. For the latest and greatest addresses, here is our pick of the best hotels in Morocco.

The pool at El Fenn in Marrakech.

Sources indicate that perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world. Jnane Rumi—the Garden of Rumi—sits squarely within this tradition in the Palmeraie, Marrakech’s historic palm grove. It was designed by Tunisian-born Charles Boccara as a private home and has just 12 rooms: 7 in the mansion, 4 garden pavilions, and 1 private villa. Boccara grew up in Casablanca and graduated from the Beaux-Arts de Paris, and this mini manor house—with its arches and domes, expressive use of local materials, and elegantly ­mullioned windows that connect the house with a glorious garden of centenarian palms and pistachio trees—embodies his elegant Euro-Maghrebi style. It’s a seductive oasis that ­naturally gathers life, which is why owners Gert-Jan van den Bergh, an art-restitution lawyer, and his somatic-therapist wife, Corinne, felt compelled to transform it into a ­cultural hub, platforming contemporary Moroccan artists and designers, and curating art events and creative retreats. —Paula Hardy.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Check Availability at Priceline.

Set between the mountains and the sea, this smart family-friendly resort and discreet spa retreat was conceived and built by King Mohammed VI as a showcase for the artisanal skills and flair that are a cornerstone of Morocco’s cultural heritage. The Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay houses more than 2,000 works of art in an astounding showcase for Moroccan craftsmanship and artisanal skills. Set on a 700-meter private beachfront along the so-called Moroccan Riviera, it sits low within a landscaped garden scented with rosemary, sage lavender, and mint. While there are some substantial name resorts further along the coastline including Sofitel and Ritz Carlton, this the first home-grown luxury offering and stands head and shoulders above the others for its service (all staff are trained at Royal Mansour’s own hospitality school) and obsessive attention to detail, as well as its sustainable practices. It’s also open year-round for dedicated spa-goers who come for Longevity programs of varying time frames in the largest and most professional med spa in Northern Africa. —Catherine Fairweather.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, successfully incorporating beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxury in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a spot of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with the city itself being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the newly opened spa, which has a thorough menu and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards. There’s an effortless blending of old and new, and a devotion to looking after the guest. Palatial, imposing, luxurious, with an impressive attention to detail, Four Seasons’ newest Moroccan property makes you feel like a modern day sultan. —Matt Charlton.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Three years after opening La Sultana Marrakech in 2004, the owners sought a quieter, more intimate spot to unveil their second Moroccan hotel. The result was La Sultana’s beachy sanctuary of restorative wellness, slotted between acres of flourishing farmland and a tranquil lagoon sheltered from the roaring Atlantic. Sustainable, sea-to-table dining is central to the La Sultana experience, and seafood lovers will be glad to hear that oysters are the star dish, with five oyster beds scattered across the lagoon. All rooms have their own elegant personality, and with just 12 to choose from, the precision which has gone into each design is palpable. The Treehouse Suite is a personal favorite, centred around a real eucalyptus tree which permeates through the bedroom floor and ceiling. There’s a lovely cathedral-inspired spa exclusive to guests, with pool, hot tub, sauna, and five treatment rooms, as well as a nearly 150-foot infinity pool outside, seamlessly seeping into the sea at high tide. —Layla Quaedvlieg.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

The rocky sparseness of Morocco’s Agafay desert has long attracted travelers wanting a break from the sensory explosions of Marrakech. It’s an ideal landing spot for the Habitas group, which since 2016 has been setting up its minimalist, sustainable eco-retreats in places like Mexico, Namibia, and Saudi Arabia. Their oasis among the lunar dunes eschews bells and whistles in favor of communal vibes and engagement with nature—or “luxury for the soul,” as the founders call it. They've now applied their ethos to Agafay’s 41 Berber-inspired tents and lodges. Each en suite tent—solar-powered, with eco-bathrooms—embodies stylish pared-down-ness: no minibars or TVs, just wooden floors and earthy cream and ochre tones reminiscent of the regional rock.

Sources indicate that weekenders escaping European cities sink into poufs and Berber rugs inside the communal glass-wrapped lounge. On the semi-open dining veranda, beneath raffia lamps, they tuck into lamb slow-cooked in the underground oven before knocking back market sangrias by the open-air bar, silhouetted against the Atlas Mountains and flame-red sunsets that give way to heavenly constellations. This is what travel is about—less guilt and more meaning amid tranquillity, good conversation, and cleansing nature. —Noo Saro-Wiwa.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that with a name as reputable as Nobu on the door, good service, and an even better restaurant offering are practically scribed into the brickwork. Marrakech is the brand's first foray into Africa, and its interiors remain respectful of the location, capturing a different kind of aesthetic that sets it apart from its Mediterranean cousins. The location is one to celebrate. From here, you can walk to the medina and the souks, or arrange drivers to take you further afield via the concierge, who suggests tours to the Atlas mountains, desert picnics, and cultural experiences like camel rides. The rooftop is as beautiful as the 360-degree views it offers, and watching the sun cast ombre shades of pink and orange across the sky before it sinks behind the horizon is best accompanied by a signature cocktail or a serving of mint tea—poured from an elaborate silver-tone pot, of course. Every bedroom is a suite bedecked in mahogany wood and rich furnishings. —Sarah Leigh Bannerman.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

According to recent reports, at the Royal Mansour Marrakech, located inside the medina, the draw is privacy—its beautifully tiled riads have their own pools dotting lush gardens that are made for afternoon strolls. The palatial resort, founded by King Mohammed VI to showcase the best of Moroccan artistry and hospitality, was built over three years by 1,200 master craftsmen. It’s a swoon-worthy showpiece of Moroccan decorative art.

In a recent development, each of the 53 individual three-story riads comprises a mini courtyard (with a canopy that automatically unfurls if rain is detected); a sumptuously appointed living room; an equally dazzling bedroom with silk-covered walls, hand-painted arched doorways, and generous MarocMaroc bath amenities; and a private rooftop terrace with a fireplace. Guests are tended to by a gracious staff, in particular a butler who appears silently through the riad’s kitchen service entry.

In a recent development, although Djemaa el Fna square is within walking distance, there’s much to keep you ensconced in this city sanctuary, including indoor and outdoor pools, a magnificent spa, and two superb restaurants, La Grande Table Marocaine and La Grande Table Française , as well as the indoor-outdoor La Table, which serves a formally presented breakfast and lunch by white-gloved staff. —Todd Plummer.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

In a recent development, this is where Charlie Chaplin and Churchill chose to hole up, and Hitchcock filmed The Man Who Knew Too Much. Reinvigorated by designer Jacques Garcia, it had a spectacular reopening in 2009. Retreat from the hubbub to the huge gardens, with their beekeepers, lemon trees, secret ice-cream parlor, and the loveliest pool with a palm tree in the middle. The Sunday poolside brunch—tagines, grilled fish, pizza flatbreads—is excellent for hungry children, as is eating in Le Marocain to the sounds of a traditional oud (a bit like a lute). For a riad-style stay, there are three houses on the grounds, but the rooms with views out to the Koutoubia Mosque and over the rooftops of the Red City are the ones that give you the best sense of place. Pick up neon earthenware jugs, Berber-style rugs, and baskets at Latest York designer Martin Raffone’s MaisonLAB in Guéliz.

Check Availability at Hotels.com.

Industry observers note that all kasbahs are a kind of oasis of calm behind fortified walls, and Kasbah Tamadot is one of the very finest in Morocco. Its name means “soft breeze” in the local Berber language, evoking the reprieve it offers in the shadow of the Atlas Mountains. First built over a century ago as a home for a local governor, it became part of the Virgin Limited Edition Collection in 2005. Now reopened following substantial damage from the 2023 earthquake, Tamadot is a lavish yet quirky Amazigh castle with exquisite carved doors and intimate courtyards, secret passageways, and terraces of reflecting pools strewn with rose petals.

Sources indicate that it's furnished with the extraordinary collections of the previous owner, a Venetian antiquarian named Luciano Tempo, which were included when Richard Branson purchased the place. Huge bronze and wooden chests that might have carried Barbarossa’s loot stand in corners. In rambling gardens, pathways meander beneath trellises of jasmine while apple trees frame the cabanas around the swimming pool. In addition to atmospheric rooms in the old kasbah, accommodations offer a step-up in luxury with 10 glamorous Berber tents in the gardens and six luxurious riads (lovely three-bedroom suites with private pools). —Stanley Stewart.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Integrating opulence in just the right measure is a difficult task, but this five-star hotel (once home to the king's advisor) pulls it off perfectly. After you enter the building with its cream-colored walls, you’ll find yourself in the lobby, a luminous space with nearly 40-foot ceilings. It’s the first hint that this hotel does everything in style: from the eight acres of landscaped grounds to the dramatic lamps that illuminate the corridor leading to the Crudo restaurant and the photogenic swimming pool, where you’ll lose track of time under the Mediterranean sun.

The hotel’s 133 rooms are an amalgam of elements that celebrate the country’s craft traditions with fretwork wooden screens, mosaics, and bespoke fabrics created by local artisans. The Fairmont Tazi Palace’s massive wellness center includes 10 treatment rooms, a private spa, a solarium, a hammam you won’t want to leave, and sunny Andalusian-style gardens that lead to a secluded vitality pool. Let yourself unwind before refueling at one of the four restaurants, where ingredients are pulled from the hotel’s own orchard and kitchen garden. —Lidia González.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It’s easy to forget what a game-changer El Fenn was when it opened two decades ago on the edge of the medina with just six jewel-toned bedrooms and a rooftop that felt like a fabulous house party. It stitched itself into the fabric of the Red City and redefined its aesthetic with color-clashing walls and lounges of thickly woven Berber and velvet fabrics, Moorish keyhole archways, and orange trees.

According to recent reports, like the best hotels, it has moved—and expanded—with the times. Co-owner Vanessa Branson has gradually bought up the crumbling neighboring riads to create a wondrous labyrinth of 13 interconnected buildings, 3 pools, and 41 bedrooms in blush pinks, mustards, and acid yellows. Some have zellige tiles, others hand-stitched camel leather floors and carved wooden ceilings, all offset with pop art and bright contemporary installations.

I recently stayed in one of the “cozy” rooms, behind an ornate cedar door. Between the hand-plastered traditional tadelakt wall, contemporary dot painting, and mother-of-pearl chandelier, it’s nearly impossible to tell old from upcoming, a result of using local artisans, natural fabrics, and upcycled furniture. Amid the rooftop’s pool, sunbeds and pops of color, the old magic of Marrakech endures. —Chloe Sachdev.

Sources indicate that connecting with nature in Morocco's beauty spot, where you can be as active or as laid-back as you like, all while enjoying the breathtaking backdrop of the Atlas Mountains. Just 20 minutes outside the heart of Marrakech, the landscape starts to change—countless olive groves, tall leafy palms, and fragrant argan and lemon trees. The distant views of the Atlas Mountains paint the scene, but it's the grand arch at the resort’s entrance that sets the tone of sheer majesty. Step through the iconic Fairmont swinging doors and you’re greeted by towering ceilings, marble accents, plush furnishings, and an endless sense of chic glamour.

The main bar, Le Bar, dressed in a sleek black-and-gold scheme, feels like a scene straight out of a James Bond film. Jaw-dropping Moroccan chandeliers add to the extravagant spirit and five-star quality. Outside, 570 acres of lush green landscape await, showcasing Marrakech’s horticultural prowess. Home to an 18-hole golf course and a pampering spa, it’s the ultimate base for wellness seekers, romantic couples, families, and culture vultures keen to experience the crème de la crème of Marrakech’s idyllic rural scene.

It has been revealed that this rare palm-framed fantasyland near Ouarzazate, whose name translates from Arabic as “House of Dreams,” was conjured20 years ago, from the wild imagination of a Parisian creative. Thierry Teyssier re-envisaged the 200-year-old ochre kasbah and its rammed-earth ramparts to honor its Berber heritage with authenticity, elegance, and an unrivaled romance. Spells at the hideaway are more magical than ever, with the handful of rooms in the North African castle joined by spacious suites at the edge of the Louis Benech–landscaped grounds.

Sources indicate that teyssier’s past lives as a theater actor and event planner keep him challenging traditional hospitality as a disrupter and storyteller: Every soul-stirring scene is art-directed and choreographed to enchant, with delicate, tactile interiors, seductive scents, and unexpected curios at every turn. Surrendering to Dar Ahlam’s rare rhythm is akin to participating in immersive theatre, with unprompted poolside pomegranate juices, candlelit Berber tents for secret suppers, and personally addressed hand-penned scrolls or other gifts at bedtime. Guests can explore vast desert-scapes by four-by-four, or let the staff plan a picnic in a villager’s vegetable garden. There is no lobby, restaurant, or bar, just beautiful spaces unfettered by telephones, menus, or minibars. —Juliet Kinsman.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

According to recent reports, royal Mansour, owned by Morocco’s royal family, can be credited as one of Marrakech’s (if not Morocco’s) finest stays: a romantic riad, where luxury is distinctly of the old-world variety. Naturally, the announcement of a second location sent the travel industry into a titter. Heads up, though: Anyone expecting a mirror image of Royal Mansour Marrakech is going to be surprised. While the level of service and luxury at the new location (in the once-home of the 1953-built El Mansour hotel) follows the first property’s lead, the experience, and especially the aesthetic, is a departure. There are 149 rooms, with three categories of suites, and several “apartment” offerings.

There are four restaurants: The brasserie serves delicious French classics, and at the sushi bar, chefs from Japan take on the task of bringing omakase to a Moroccan audience. For Moroccan food, head up to the 23rd floor. Just before sunset, the room of mirrors and gold comes alive in the light. Stick around for delicious sweet baghrir bread, fried spinach cheese briouat, and naturally, more tajines. The views over the city aren’t bad either. —Megan Spurrell.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

How we choose the best hotels in Morocco.

Recent findings suggest that every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

In a recent development, if you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health strategy, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

In a recent development, the travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just introduced what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Sources indicate that but who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really swiftly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the strategy can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Recent findings suggest that health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Recent findings suggest that parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking latest income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
  • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

Sources indicate that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he remarked when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” stated Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” noted Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he noted, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Industry observers note that zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

Recent findings suggest that the Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with prepares to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

In a recent development, zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Industry observers note that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a organization registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

According to recent reports, since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which states it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he noted, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom revealed Friday.

Sources indicate that seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

“He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

Recent findings suggest that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

According to recent reports, gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

In a recent development, american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A fresh reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

“For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

The 10 Best Places to Retire in the US

  • According to recent reports, it’s all about living life your way and celebrating your passions.
  • To help guide that decision, WalletHub has released its annual Best & Worst Places to Retire list—a ranking of 182 cities across the US (including the 150 most populated US cities, plus at least two of the most populated cities in each state) based on affordability, activities, quality of life, and healthcare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these days, retirement can come in many different forms—and arrive at many different ages. Some may choose to spend their golden years indulging in new hobbies, sports, and skills, while others may decide to focus on spending more quality time with family or take off and travel the world.

According to recent reports, it’s all about living life your way and celebrating your passions. But no matter when you choose to pull the career plug, everyone deserves to find a home base that can best support your newfound lifestyle. After all, not being tied down to an office or career means you can finally move to your dream city, or bop between your favorite travel destinations.

To help guide that decision, WalletHub has released its annual Best & Worst Places to Retire list—a ranking of 182 cities across the US (including the 150 most populated US cities, plus at least two of the most populated cities in each state) based on affordability, activities, quality of life, and healthcare. Unsurprisingly, four Florida cities made the Top 10—including claiming all top three spots—powered by the state's tax-free policies and warm weather.

Here are the 10 best places to retire in the US, according to this year’s WalletHub study, along with supporting data we’ve pulled from the US Census Bureau, Zillow, city governments, and the demographic data firm Best Places. Whether you end up chasing sunshine or snowflakes, small towns or urban hubs, the words “retirement home” could be much more exciting than you think.

This gallery has been updated with upcoming information since its original publication date.

According to recent reports, with dramatic rivers and bridges dotting its scenery, and a culture and food scene that is constantly reinventing itself, Pittsburgh isn’t just a place to be—it’s a place to make home. Even with all the benefits of an urban hub, housing prices are generally lower than in most of the country. Pittsburgh is also known for having some of the best hospitals in the nation, with an array of social services designed to take care of senior residents. The list of activities to do here is endless, whether it’s taking the Duquesne or Monongahela inclines to see sky-high views of the river confluences, or exploring the latest exhibits at local museums like the Carnegie Museum of Art and Andy Warhol Museum, or the quirky Randyland. And of course, the food options here are diverse and delightful, from Italian neighborhood favorite DiAnoia’s Eatery to take-out from Lucy’s Banh Mi, lovingly made and served out of a makeshift trailer.

Population: 302,971 (median age: 34.4 years).

Industry observers note that cost of living: The median home price is $234,620, over $130,000 less than the national median. Rent is also significantly lower, with the average being $1,550.

Sources indicate that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 160 sunny days per year; average lows of 21°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

Healthcare: Pittsburgh has 38.1 physicians per 10,000 residents, above the US average.

Honestly, could there be a better place to retire? Charleston is the best of every world, starting with a burgeoning culinary scene. Among the standouts are southern staples like Miller’s All Day and Callie’s Hot Little Biscuit, seafood spots like Leon’s Oyster Shop and Hank’s Seafood Restaurant, and modern favorites Chubby Fish, Frannie and the Fox, and Bar 167. Add to that a walkable downtown (including the local open-air market hall Charleston City Market) and waterfront (with the iconic Pineapple Fountain!).

Population: 150,227 (median age: 36.6 years).

Cost of living: The median home cost in Charleston is $587,511—about 1.6 the national median. The average rent is $3,000 (an increase of about $100 since last year).

It has been revealed that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 209 sunny days per year; average lows of 39°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

Healthcare: Charleston has 47.8 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

According to recent reports, while Fort Lauderdale may be best known for its beaches, the city’s appeal extends far beyond the coastline these days. With a plethora of waterfront condos to call home, days can be spent touring art galleries in Flagler Village, taking cooking classes at Sistrunk Market, or birding at Hugh Taylor Birch State Park and Secret Woods Nature Center. Plus, sports fans will love the roster of teams to cheer on, like soccer and hockey—and Miami Heat and Miami Dolphins’ home stadiums are both a short drive away.

Population: 182,760 (median age: 42.5 years).

It has been revealed that cost of living: The median home cost in Fort Lauderdale is $509,743—a slight drop from last year, but still much higher than the national median. The average rent is $2,700 (an increase of about $100 since last year).

It has been revealed that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 246 sunny days per year; average lows of 59°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

Healthcare: Fort Lauderdale has 22.4 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

As long as you can tolerate some mightily cold winters, retiring in Minneapolis means you’re never far from great independent retailers, worthwhile museums, scenic lakes, and dining experiences that extend far beyond the tater tot hotdish. Despite falling four rankings from last year, the City of Lakes still has plenty going for it. The best part? “Minnesota nice” is a very real thing, so there’s a pretty good chance you’ll end up with a friendly neighbor.

Population: 429,954 (median age: 33.3 years).

It has been revealed that cost of living: The median home cost in Minneapolis is $328,351, which is lower than the national median. The average rent is a reasonable $1,717.

Income tax on social security? Yes.

Climate: 198 sunny days per year; average lows of 7°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

Healthcare: Minneapolis has 33.9 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

In a recent development, atlanta is chock full of activities, be it museums, sports, live music, or just getting outside and taking it all in. All that and more contributes to the Georgia capital ranking 4 out of 170 in Wallethub’s activities index. One new attraction is the Atlanta Beltline, a greenway that's right now being built around the city, which debuted its Southside and Southeast trails this year. Travel lovers will also appreciate being near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport—the busiest international airport in the world. And don’t forget to mix in the city’s innovative Southern food scene, with diverse highlights like Mary Mac’s Tea Room, Rina, and Botiwalla by Chai Pani.

Population: 498,715 (median age: 34.5 years).

In a recent development, cost of living: The median home cost in Atlanta is $380,331, which is higher than the national median. The average rent is $2,089, above the national average.

Industry observers note that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 217 sunny days per year; average lows of 33°F in winter; average highs of 88°F in summer.

Healthcare: Atlanta has 36.5 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

Recent findings suggest that if city life isn’t quite how you imagined spending your golden years, Casper, Wyoming, is perfect for those seeking a Ron Swanson-style retirement. Spend your days fly-fishing, canoeing, and hiking right outside your door—not to mention day-trip access to Grand Teton and Rocky Mountain national parks. In terms of culture, there are plenty of art museums, planetariums, and historic sites to continue that sense of exploration. As an added bonus, it’s by far one of the least expensive towns on this list—WalletHub ranked it 3rd out of 182 for affordability. It’s no wonder it leaped five spots from last year up to fifth place.

Population: 59,038 (median age: 37.3 years).

Cost of living: The median home sale price in Casper is $310,650, which is lower than the national median. The average rent is $1,350, up $150 from last year.

Sources indicate that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 220 sunny days per year; average lows of 15°F in winter; average highs of 88°F in summer.

Healthcare: Casper has 19.7 physicians per 10,000 residents (a bit below the national average).

As the No. 1 city in WalletHub's quality of life metric, Scottsdale is easily one of the best places to retire in the US, despite sinking two spots from last year. It is a famously popular spot for golfers, but it also boasts plenty of destination spas, incredible art and architecture, and James Beard Award-winning restaurants to satisfy retirees of all types. Another upside: 330 sunny days a year. Just be prepared for really, really hot summers—average temperatures from June to September are all in the triple digits.

Population: 241,361 (median age: 53 years).

Cost of living: The median home cost in Scottsdale is $851,746, which is nearly 2.3 times higher than the national median. The median rent is $3,400 per month, more than $1,400 above the national median.

Industry observers note that income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 330 sunny days per year; average lows of 42°F in winter; average highs of 104°F in summer.

Healthcare: Scottsdale has 20.1 physicians per 10,000 residents (below the national average).

Tampa, on Florida's Gulf Coast, rose two spots to capture the bronze medal this year. The city itself has plenty of housing options, a buzzing Riverwalk, and one of the best airports in the country. With plenty of surrounding suburbs, it also makes a great jumping-off point for exploring other beach towns in the state. Foodies should take note, as Tampa is known for its restaurants—Rooster & the Till (run by James Beard semi-finalist Ferrell Alvarez) and 384,959 (median age: 36.3 years) (beloved for its Cuban sandwiches) are two stand-outs.

Population: 384,959 (median age: 36.3 years).

Sources indicate that cost of living: The median home cost in Tampa is $375,619, up just 0.4 percent over last year. The average rent is $1,962/month, down $95 since last year.

Income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 246 sunny days per year; average lows of 52°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

Healthcare: Tampa has 24.3 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

Miami rose two spots since last year to the runner-up position. It may not be quite as affordable as other cities, but Miami has enough art galleries, Cuban food, golf courses, beaches, and museums to justify the rent. (And who wouldn’t love the chance to drive down to Key West whenever they want?) Miami-Dade County even offers an “Active Older Adults Program” that provides free fitness classes, games, field trips and arts activities for people ages 55 and older. Plus it ranks the sixth most walkable city on this list, with most residents having access to public transportation within walking distance of their homes.

Population: 442,241 (median age: 41.2 years).

In a recent development, cost of living: The median home cost in Miami is $583,705, which is up 1.4% from last year. The average rent is $3,100, the same as last year.

Income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 248 sunny days per year; average lows of 61°F in winter; average highs of 89°F in summer.

Healthcare: Miami has 22.8 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

For the third year in a row, Orlando snagged the trophy for the most retiree-friendly city in the nation. We’ve already mentioned the warm weather and low taxes of Florida, but Orlando has a particular abundance of quiet communities, great restaurants, and independent stores—and its inland location means you won’t have to worry quite as much during hurricane season. (Bonus: Given Orlando’s proximity to theme parks, it’ll be easy to convince family to visit, too.).

Population: 307,573 (median age: 35.4 years).

Cost of living: The median home cost in Orlando is $372,775, which is down 1.1% from last year. The average rent is $1,850/month, about $145 less than last year.

Income tax on social security? No.

Climate: 233 sunny days per year; average lows of 49°F in winter; average highs of 92°F in summer.

Healthcare: Orlando has 20.4 physicians per 10,000 residents (below the national average).

Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.
  • This time around, the complications occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.
  • The delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel prepares for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.

This time around, the complications occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.

The delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel prepares for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips. While the problem was resolved Sunday afternoon, the airline delayed 300 flights and canceled 92 flights on Monday morning, according to FlightAware. “Operations are stable today with automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations fully restored,” a Delta spokesperson told Traveler on Monday. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers.”.

For US travelers, the timing is particularly stressful. AAA projects 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights over the Thanksgiving holiday period. Plus, Delta’s operational difficulties came only nine days after the FAA declared a rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted more than four hours and led to multiple days of travel chaos.

In a recent development, while Delta’s technology concerns had nothing to do with the FAA systems, both incidents have travelers questioning if their Thanksgiving travel looks will be disrupted. Here’s a look at the current situation and what travelers should know before heading to the airport this week.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

According to recent reports, on Sunday morning, Delta began having issues with its weight and balance automation system at the Atlanta airport. The system’s critical equipment assesses whether aircraft are too heavy to fly before takeoff.

In a recent development, while the system was out, Delta crews use manual backup processes to help flights depart. However, the technology outage still led to thousands of delays and hundreds of cancellations.

Delta had 2,194 flight delays on November 22, which is about 64% of its schedule, according to FlightAware data. The carrier also had 274 canceled flights on Sunday. Although some of those disruptions were due to other challenges, like bad weather in the Northeast, Delta remarked that 70% of the flight changes were caused by the ATL equipment problems, according to CNN.

Recent findings suggest that the airline remarked it had restored the system by Sunday afternoon. By Monday morning, Delta’s flight schedules across the country appeared to be getting back on track. However, as of 11 a.m. ET on Monday, the carrier had accumulated more than 300 flight delays and 92 cancellations, FlightAware indicated. Now that the technology concern has been resolved, travelers can expect Delta's flight schedule to progressively return to normal but should still prepare for lingering delays through Tuesday, November 24.

Travelers with canceled flights can ask for a full cash refund if they no longer wish to travel. The carrier doesn’t charge passengers to change their flights if they’re booked in any fare class except basic economy (although a difference in fare may apply).

Industry observers note that passengers should continue to check with Delta for the latest information on their flight status. When traveling for Thanksgiving, err on the side of caution and strategy to arrive at the airport early: at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international one.

According to recent reports, the ground stop on November 13 was due to a separate concern with air traffic control equipment outages and the telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” claims the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”.

On November 13, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the challenges began, according to the FAA. The organization was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” claims an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”.

Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA says that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications problems are still under investigation.

Industry observers note that regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the concern. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy noted in a recent interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”.

Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of US Travel Association. The “disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”.

For many US airlines, the busy Thanksgiving travel season began with early departures on November 19 and is expected to last through December 1.

Recent findings suggest that air travel experts say that the FAA ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel prepares should be minimal. As of November 16, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. Delta was also able to restore its systems on Sunday, November 22; as of Monday, flight schedules began returning to normal but Delta fliers could still encounter lingering delays early this week.

It helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this Thanksgiving compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics tech giant, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually one of the busiest air travel days of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying.

Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop.

However, Delta is still allowing passengers who were scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16 to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Customers' new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

Even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

Sources indicate that it’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman of the US Travel Association. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages in the long run.

Industry observers note that “The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”.

Recent findings suggest that airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”.

Following the ground stop, the DOT requested an additional $50.1 billion from Congress to complete its overhaul of the national air traffic control system.

For more information on passenger rights during airline technology outages, read our full guide.

Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
  • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.
  • That means staffing up major committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, stated the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan stated.

It has been revealed that still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she states of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can swiftly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Recent findings suggest that some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

It has been revealed that there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, stated Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

According to recent reports, “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres mentioned.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the upcoming year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he remarked.

In a recent development, in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

In a recent development, lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a massive difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

It has been revealed that those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, mentioned he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

In a recent development, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal remarked he won’t be deterred by the letter.

Industry observers note that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

In a recent development, “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

Recent findings suggest that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries stated.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

It has been revealed that beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet unveiled — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

In a recent development, signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To quell this concern, the upcoming card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

#99955. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

📅 16 May 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1617 w)
