General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Godsavethepoints ↗ Open Full Page

Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

📅 16 May 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Newly introduced York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots.
  • In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies.
  • In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Newly introduced York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic released in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that states pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter organization which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

Sources indicate that the truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Recent findings suggest that everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

According to recent reports, getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

It has been revealed that on real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

Sources indicate that I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Recent findings suggest that their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

According to recent reports, the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, major airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Sources indicate that tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

Sources indicate that if Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Sources indicate that let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and manufacturer books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

Recent findings suggest that the business purports to be a home swap manufacturer, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

Sources indicate that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or latest seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC.
  • Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.
  • Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” stated Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, remarked House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

In a recent development, leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

Industry observers note that california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very problem that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

Industry observers note that “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

It has been revealed that “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido noted. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

Industry observers note that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

In a recent development, colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

Recent findings suggest that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

It has been revealed that amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto noted.

How many countries are in the Caribbean?

The Caribbean is a diverse region made up of over 700 islands, islets, reefs, and cays, but not all are independent countries. In total, there are 13 sovereign nations and 17 dependent territories spread across the Caribbean Sea. The independent countries include popular destinations such as Jamaica, the Bahamas, Barbados, St. Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago. The dependent territories—like Puerto Rico (US), Martinique (France), and the Cayman Islands (UK)—offer a mix of cultural influences and governance structures. While each island varies in size, language, and history, the entire region is united by its tropical climate, vibrant cultures, and rich mix of African, European, and Indigenous heritage.

What is the best island to visit in the Caribbean?

There isn’t one “best” Caribbean island—it just depends on what kind of experience you’re seeking. Families often love Jamaica for its all-inclusive resorts, kid-friendly activities, and easy flights from the US. Surfers gravitate toward Barbados and Puerto Rico, which boast consistent swells and a laid-back surf culture. Solo travelers often choose Puerto Rico or Curaçao, thanks to their safety, walkable cities, and friendly locals. For romantic getaways, St. Lucia and Antigua are top picks—think private villas, lush rainforests, and stunning beaches perfect for couples. And for multi-generational trips, the Bahamas or Turks and Caicos stand out, offering luxury accommodations, calm beaches for kids, and plenty of excursions for all ages. Each island has its own rhythm and charm, so the “best” one depends on your travel style and interests.

When is the best time to travel to the Caribbean?

The best time to visit the Caribbean typically falls between December and April, during the region’s dry season. This period offers warm temperatures, low humidity, and minimal rainfall—ideal conditions for beach days and outdoor adventures. However, it’s also the peak tourist season, meaning higher prices and more crowds. For travelers seeking better deals and fewer tourists, the shoulder months of May, June, and November are excellent alternatives, offering good weather with occasional rain showers. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, and while severe storms are rare on most islands, it’s wise to stay informed about forecasts if traveling during this time.

Which islands in the Caribbean are the most affordable?

Jamaica and the Dominican Republic are good places to start if you're looking for budget-friendly rentals. But keep in mind that no matter which island you head to, the neighborhood and season you're traveling in matter just as much as anything else, and an exclusive beachfront address can swiftly change your budget. To get the most bang for your buck, consider traveling during shoulder or off seasons, and take a look at rentals outside of the typical tourist hot spots.

Are there any islands in the Caribbean you can visit from the US without a passport?

According to recent reports, yes. US citizens traveling directly from the mainland can visit Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands without a passport. The US Virgin Islands include St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, and travelers can also head to Puerto Rico’s offshore islands of Vieques and Culebra.

Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India.
  • On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was declared with very interesting nods to the future.
  • IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was declared with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

According to recent reports, that’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a fresh manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are massive business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

Industry observers note that in a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local firm, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

According to recent reports, when asked about loyalty implications of the fresh alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following….

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

In a recent development, to me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

According to recent reports, in short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

Industry observers note that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

Industry observers note that in the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

Industry observers note that but now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

Sources indicate that and the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

Recent findings suggest that as an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

In a recent development, naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight?
  • Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its fresh corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

Industry observers note that the fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s latest branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

It has been revealed that the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Industry observers note that iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the latest changes.

Sources indicate that the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

But what about the redemption of points?

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

In a recent development, which leads me to the key bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a latest “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Sources indicate that previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the fresh version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

In a recent development, I am in Latest York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive….

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

It has been revealed that A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

According to recent reports, if Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the fresh 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

At Traveler, the titles we swear by take us through H Mart with an expert guide at hand to break down the aisles, to Sri Lanka, where the palette of London hot spot Hoppers was formed, and to the sugar-dusted counters of Broma Bakery, where Sarah Fennel has the key to 100 desserts sure to satisfy any sweet tooth. The best cookbooks immerse you in the corner of the world they come from, and through their pages, narrative transforms into a multi-sensory experience. Just as we're placing finishing touches on our holiday menus, our editors gathered their favorite cookbooks of all time that take readers all across the map, from recent releases that have become instant classics in our households to vintage volumes that continue to stand the test of time.

We'd love to hear about the cookbooks that take a place of pride in your kitchen on Instagram or Facebook.

According to recent reports, I was lucky enough to taste chef Ifrah Ahmed's food at a beautiful dinner last year, so I couldn't wait to add her cookbook Soomaaliya to my shelf when it came out this spring. In Somalia, she writes, "knowledge is passed down orally," but she records the flavors and traditions of the culture in this stunning homage to Somalia's rich culinary legacy. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

Sources indicate that when I’m working my way through a recipe or just slapping something together for the sake of a pantry clean-out, odds are that the secret ingredient that ties it all together is an item I picked up at H Mart. Perhaps it’s the splash of Shaoxing cooking wine that makes all the notes in a fried rice sing that much more, or the half-packet of Buldak sauce that brings on the much-needed heat to some peanut noodles. As a card-carrying fan of the brand, I was ecstatic when I learned H Mart co-president Stacey Kwon had committed the splendor of the Korean grocery store’s aisles to pages in a cookbook. Beyond just housing recipes (the Galbi Jjim is a dinner party show-stopper), this omnibus also lets readers in on the store’s history, the tips and tricks of navigating its inventory, and handy guides that will have you cooking like it's second nature. This volume is a boon for H Mart enthusiasts and a fantastic tool for those just beginning their journey in the kitchen. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

It has been revealed that I love Hoppers, the dish. I love Hoppers, the homey London restaurant chain dishing out delicious Sri Lankan and southern Indian fare. So it’s a no-brainer that I love cooking from Hoppers, the cookbook. With the recipes in this book, author and restaurant owner Karan Gokani attempts to make traditional dishes like lamb kari and buriani feel approachable, all with the trademark come-join-me affability of his Instagram cooking videos. Some of these recipes are Proustian madeleines, taking me back to early-morning visits to fish markets in southern India or the many holidays spent along Sri Lanka’s southern coast, as well as to my grandmother’s dining table in Kerala. There’s a striking overlap in ingredients and flavors when it comes to Kerala and Sri Lanka, and it’s always a pleasure to get to sample that shared heritage. Now, if only I could summon a supply of the Arrack Attack cocktails from Hoppers as I cooked… —Arati Menon, global digital director.

Since I’ve moved to New York, I’ve known that whenever I’m looking for a taste of home, I can always head to the East Village or Williamsburg to Taiwanese-American restaurant Win Son (and its bakery off-shoots). And now with the restaurant’s cookbook, I can recreate their lu rou fan (braised pork rice) or tsang ying tou (fly’s head, a fragrant mix of pork and chives that goes over rice) for myself. I’m fortunate to have grown up with a mom who was a fantastic cook, but the magic she worked in the kitchen has always been obscure to me. She’s true to the trope of never writing any recipes down, instead relying on muscle memory and years of road-tested intuition. But with the wisdom of Ku, Brown, and Erway’s book by my side, I’ve finally been able to master my childhood dishes and resist the urge to order takeout. —K.C.

I became interested in plant-based dining once I started dating a vegan, and one of the first restaurants that opened my eyes to all the possibilities of letting go of meat was Amanda Cohen’s Dirt Candy. It’s one of my favorite restaurants in the whole city, with a seasonal tasting menu that doesn’t break the bank but still stretches your imagination by showing you the full flavor spectrum of a leek, or proving by example that yes, eggplant really does belong in a dessert. Their cookbook is an absolute joy to read through, especially since it’s part comic book! It’s as fun as it is revelatory, and it’s a showcase of how cooking is an art as well as a form of play. —K.C.

Sources indicate that A friend gifted me Table for Two when my partner and I moved in together a few years ago. It was sweet, and the cover added some much-needed color and beauty to my kitchen counter. But its not just a pretty face—this cookbook has challenged me. From slow-cooked lamb and cinnamon stew to fluffy, peach crepes, these recipes are made to impress. You’ll find a mix of one-pan meals, specialty dinners, delicious lunches, and rich desserts. If you’re trying to win someone over, this cookbook will help you every step of the way. —M.K.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to educational heroes, Alton Brown is on the pediment alongside Bill Nye and LeVar Burton for me. Watching his show Good Eats on Food Network was a formative ritual; he just has this infectious geekiness about him. As a sort of food mad scientist, Brown can be technical bordering on obsessive, but it’s that attention to detail that makes his methods so approachable: cooking is something you can break down to its basics and understand. This first volume is all about the fundamentals, and with it you’ll never make a bad batch of brownies or dry turkey again. —K.C.

I stumbled upon this vintage cookbook at a secondhand bookstore, and I initially purchased it as a novelty item. I’d never seen a cookbook dedicated to an appliance before, let alone one I had never associated with “cooking” to begin with. But much like how I’d imagine Methven’s initial readership reacted in 1978, I was pleasantly shocked and excited by how versatile the microwave really is. There are recipes ranging from Scallops Au Gratin to Barbecue Ribs to Seven-Minute Brownies in this book, and I’ve gleaned many staples from its pages. It’s only right to acknowledge you’re not going to get restaurant-quality versions or true-to-form authenticity out of every dish, but if you’re wiling to adventure, this is one of the most accessible ways to do it from your own home. Sometimes when I’m at a loss for what to make and feeling sluggish, I’ll perform a little bibliomancy on this book to figure out lunch. Even if you’re just interested in this title for your coffee table, the photography is beautiful and occasionally experimental in its efforts to display the science behind the fresh-fangled microwave. —K.C.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows….

Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
  • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move promptly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

Sources indicate that “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

In a recent development, “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries remarked. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have mentioned they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries mentioned Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

It has been revealed that this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

On Location: Dig Stars Amy Poehler and Geraldine Viswanathan on Italian Gelato, Go-Karting—and Tailgating

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1382 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television highlights, and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens.
  • Sources indicate that “The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very crucial structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television highlights, and more. This time, we take a look at Dig.

Recent findings suggest that amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens. So she took her first trip there to set the scene for her 10-part Peacock comedy series Dig, which drops November 23.

Sources indicate that “The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very crucial structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler. “The old and the fresh are constantly bumping up against each other. It was very cool to be there and really helped remind us of the theme of the show that the past is just around the corner and you can't hide from it.”.

According to recent reports, each of the characters comes to the dig site at different stage of their life, with Poehler as an archaeologist stuck as second fiddle to beloved Neville (Hugh Laurie). But it’s her bond with fellow diggers, heartbroken free spirit Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), young and flustered Patty (Fina Strazza), and refined but ready to rebel Clare (Antonia Thomas) that provides the backbone of the series—a coming of age story for every age.

Despite being set purely in Greece, Poehler states they quickly found that “Puglia wine country, Greece, and Los Angeles can kind of double for each other, which is weird." So the team made southeastern Italy their home base, checking in at Rocco Forte's Masseria Torre Maizza, where they indulged in seafood (“We got overwhelmed by how good the food was!”) and bought tons of pottery wherever they traveled, a side effect of talking about it on the show so much.

According to recent reports, off-set, they found high-speed fun, thanks to the keen ears of Laurie. “We could hear the roar of go-karts from our hotel, so he went around on a motorbike—he's so cool—and found this place,” Viswanathan indicates of Circuit Kart Evolution in Fasano. Poehler jumps in: “The crew and most of the cast raced, but a couple of outsider Europeans who snuck in ended up winning because they had the real lead foot!”.

Amy Poehler's 10-part Peacock series films all across the Mediterranean.

In a recent development, as for where a second season could take them, the cast will only drop hints. Viswanathan states it will be “a little spicier," while Poehler adds “it would be more passionate and fiery." But one thing's for sure, they are ready to start digging again soon. "We have some ideas for where to go and what kind of stuff we could dig up,” Poehler says. “Archeological digs are in a lot of different countries, so we could go all over!”.

Recent findings suggest that with her executive producer hat on, Poehler really honed in on the details of Greek culture during her time in Athens, in order to capture that same essence on screen. “I’m a New Yorker, so Athens is a really cool, vibrant, interesting city, but it does have a lot more graffiti than we expected,” she admits, adding that “some of it is really beautiful.” That meant they had to add that grittiness to some of their recreated sets in Italy and California. Another unique aspect: “the light in Greece is so specific and beautiful,” she claims of the natural rays. The best part? “We got to wrap and then go have the best salad you’d ever had in your life—I’m still thinking about it.” Her favorite was a meal at Barbounaki, where “the guy basically mentioned trust me and came back with a whole fish and cut it at the table—it was so good.”.

The fifth-century BCE Temple of Poseidon serves as an epic ancient backdrop in Dig.

It has been revealed that just over an hour’s drive southeast of Athens stands the remains of the Doric-style Temple of Poseidon, dating back to the mid-fifth century BCE, where Poehler and Laurie filmed. “Talk about set decoration—you’re standing in front of something so amazing,” she states of the ruins at the end of Cape Sounion overlooking the Aegean Sea. The sacred place is even mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey, so needless to say, it’s also a busy tourist attraction. “We had to get there at the crack of dawn before the tours,” Poehler says, noting that the landmark’s staff was standing behind them counting down the minutes they had left. “That’s tough when you’re doing an emotional scene and you know someone wants to get you out of there.” But eventually they did have to open to the public as the cameras kept rolling. “It was funny to be pretending to have this conversation when there’s an American tourist behind you in the shot eating a bag of jelly beans.”.

In a recent development, the port town of Monopoli provided the rich seaside vibe to double as Greece. Viswanathan states the initial montage where viewers are introduced to her character Dylan when she wakes up on a bench and asks for directions to the dig site was all in town, “which was so dreamy.” Poehler particularly loved the shopping scenes in its old town, including one with Laurie, shot at the hat shop Castrignano dal 1923 (sharp-eyed viewers will see it retains its Italian signage despite being set in Greece). “We wanted a place that Neville would go to pick out his hat for the year, and of course because it’s Italy, there was a beautiful old hat store in the middle of Monopoli and we used some of their hats.”.

At Polignano a Mare, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept open a local gelato stand for the public to enjoy free scoops.

Known for its dramatic scenery and crescent beaches, Polignano a Mare is best remembered to the duo for its most famous treat. “Gelato, so much gelato—Amy let the whole town eat gelato,” Viswanathan revealed. Indeed, after filming at a stand in town, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept it open for the public to enjoy free scoops too. “Then Mike reminded me that I have not paid my half,” she admits. Despite being lactose intolerant, Viswanathan has a sweet spot for hazelnut, while Poehler is all about stracciatella, a refined form of chocolate chip. “I have to say, as an American, chocolate chip is very hard to find—it’s being replaced by mint chip,” to which her co-star replies, “ That’s so not right.”.

The crew also headed inland to the hilltop town of Carovigno with a medieval fortress and a compact city center, which provided the bones for their set. “The locals were very interested in the fact that a production came in and shut down their town square and changed all of the store signs to Greek,” Poehler indicates. Viswanathan adds: “They were like, these Americans are confused—and lost!” But to get there, they also had to navigate the distinctly Italian way of driving. “It was intense—they come up really close and tailgate in a real way,” Poehler stated. “You’ve got to get out of the way!”.

Some of the Mediterranean scenery was recreated on a Universal Studios backlot in California.

Industry observers note that back on the Universal Studios backlot, set designer Dan Bishop—who’s worked on Mad Men and Parks and Recreation—recreated the Greek settings and dig site. “He and his team went over to Greece and got a bunch of local beer and signs, so when we were shooting in Los Angeles, it was really fun to be around all the stuff that felt authentic, from the colors and flowers to the buildings—it’s really notable to get a feel of that.” But there was one twist that was distinctly Hollywood. “At times we could hear the Fast and Furious: [Hollywood Drift] roller coaster while we were shooting,” Poehler said of the theme park ride that opened in September, after they filmed. “We were hearing them do test runs—it’s open now, which is really exciting,” Viswanathan claims. While she hadn't been on it yet, she commented, “the night is young.” As for Poehler, she's most happy with her feet firmly on the ground.

Industry News: The Best Shopping in Athens for Crafts, Old and Fresh

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Resplendent, timeless Athens is no stranger to feats of invention and imagination.
  • The Acropolis rises over Monastiraki Square and Tzistarakis Mosque.
  • Recent findings suggest that following a stint in Paris designing for Jean Paul Gaultier and Kenzo over 25 years ago, Lito Karakostanoglou set up her jewelry brand, Lito, in Kolonaki.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Resplendent, timeless Athens is no stranger to feats of invention and imagination. From the hand-carved marble stelae and temple friezes of the stately Acropolis to painted terra-cotta vessels unearthed throughout Attica, this is a city with millennia's worth of artistic output. You'll see this legacy on full display today in the museums and galleries that protect its artifacts. But, crucially, a upcoming wave of makers are sculpting ceramics, weaving baskets, and vigorously curating heirlooms for the contemporary eye. There is plenty to discover in the historic center—at Monastiraki's sprawling outdoor market and ceramics studios, and Syntagma's perfumeries—though that's only the start. Athens may be among the world's oldest cities, but in bustling flea markets and quiet showrooms, its many creatives are paving the path forward.

The Acropolis rises over Monastiraki Square and Tzistarakis Mosque.

Recent findings suggest that following a stint in Paris designing for Jean Paul Gaultier and Kenzo over 25 years ago, Lito Karakostanoglou set up her jewelry brand, Lito, in Kolonaki. Treat the boutique and its nature-inspired offerings as a cabinet of curiosities. The showroom upstairs is your go-to for one-off pieces. Meanwhile, renowned family jeweler Lalaounis, on Voukourestiou Street, contains glittering collections that take cues from Nubian and Hellenistic art. Harder to find, but easier on the purse, is Neso Studio, in a prewar residential building on Praxitelous. Gold, gold-plated, and silver pieces are handmade there using wax casting techniques. It's best to check ahead for opening times.

Former managing director of label Yiorgos Eleftheriades, Yiorgos Mo turned his knack for collecting into Mo Vintage Athens in 2020. At his tiny shop in arty Koukaki, nab designer pieces from the 1970s to '90s—keep an eye out for Mugler rarities. A 20-minute walk north will take you to L'On, focusing on '80s and '90s garb; think Armani bodysuits and denim sprinkled amid garments from lesser-known Greek labels. Among Psirri's graffiti-sprayed shutters a few blocks over, shop custom-designed Mantility silk scarves and Homatino ceramics on display at Monument Hotel Athens. Nearby, hat workshop Savapile, led by Lisa Sarigiannidou, is the only remaining straw-hat maker in Greece still sewing Italian braid with traditional millinery techniques.

Sheep’s wool kilim and handloomed carpets are draped on a wall of Anthologist.

In eclectic Monastiraki, Mon Coin Studio—which features works from some 300 Greek ceramists—is equally varied. Its collaborative efforts culminate in three annual group shows, one of which is always dedicated to a region rich with a ceramics past such as Sifnos, Lesbos, or Crete. Head north to Vathi for blown-glass amphorae and handloomed throws at Anthologist; it's likely founder Andria Mitsakos will offer you tea and dates as you peruse. South of the Acropolis, shop at Ere Athens, where you can tuck into a cappuccino and banana bread (a perk of going to a store that's run by a pastry chef) while browsing locally made pottery neatly laid atop wood cabinets. Popular picks include paint-splattered cake stands by potter Nicola Fasano and painterly vases from Naked Summers.

Founded by brothers Giorgos and Apostolis Korres, The Naxos Apothecary near Syntagma Square creates tinctures and creams inspired by the Med. Scientific vessels and cloaked candles decorate the space, populated by staff wearing navy lab coats reminiscent of an old-school pharmacy. Leave no display case unexplored, then head upstairs for the herbal tea bar and an outpost of label Ancient Greek Sandals. Just as curated is perfume boutique and florist Phāon in Kolonaki, owned by art director and set designer duo Alexandros Kalogiros and Dimitra Louana Marlanti. Here, find soaps and scents from Astier de Villatte and Ormaie Paris, as well as golden candlesticks by Vasiliki and ceramic lotus flowers courtesy of Despina Charitonidi. Gnocchi the Jack Russell gives everyone a warm welcome.

Hyper Hypo’s selection of books.

According to recent reports, noting a lack of art and design bookshops in the city, graphic designer Stathis Mitropoulos and former fashion editor Andreas Kokkino opened their own. Hyper Hypo, meaning “above and below,” offers literature on photography, interior design, local culture, and more. Dimitris Papaioannou's Sketches From Life, drawn over three summers in Anafi, and Eleanor Lines's illustrated Doors of Kypseli stand out against the Aegean blue walls, while a pair of neon-lit eyes glow above the counter. Plus, Hyper Hypo's seasonal event programming and rare book pop-ups make a visit all the more memorable.

Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
  • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
  • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

According to recent reports, hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

Industry observers note that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an crucial part of it.”.

According to recent reports, “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” noted Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

It has been revealed that “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very firm that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson stated. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a organization’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

Recent findings suggest that myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also mentioned that Hawley’s newly introduced arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles stated. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.
