    #99936. Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2019 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection.
    • Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026.
    • Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection. My stay was almost exactly 24 hours and solo which is uncharacteristic at this destination resort. My experience will likely differ from other guests due to those factors.

    Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026. It sits on a stretch of white-sand beach in Costa Mujeres, 12 miles north of Cancun. Cancun International Airport is the arrival airport. I could not confirm a single official transfer time from the property page. Tour listings commonly put the drive in a 30 to 45 minute range.

    Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.

    Google Maps: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres.

    Hyatt is the best in the business at high end resort arrivals. I had given my name at the security gate and by the time I reached the lobby, the door to the vehicle was opened for me, I was greeted by name and a “welcome home”, a constant refrain throughout my stay. It’s a small thing and maybe cliché but it was effective. I was given a Globalist upgrade even though rules at all-inclusives differ from the rest of the chain. As my upgrade was in a Preferred room, I was brought into a private room at the front of the lobby where check-in was done for me.

    The lobby is an open-air room under an arched woven ceiling, with a direct view out to the ocean.

    According to recent reports, the resort is spread across 10 buildings with 505 keys. Of those, 221 are Preferred Club keys with an elevated experience. My building (and others like it) had just five rooms on each floor and just five floors which made it feel boutique rather than massive. Every oceanfront room is Preferred Club, and so are the first two buildings on either side.

    The room views follow a simple rule by floor. Every first floor room is a swim-out, floors two through four are tropical view, and the fifth floor is ocean view or ocean front. That makes booking easy to reason through: if you want to step off your patio into the water, go low, and if you want the sea, go high.

    The walkways give a sense of grandeur and space. All of the flora is local, and in a touch I loved, the service rooms are named after the plants.

    It has been revealed that there are four pools, and each one has a unique characteristic. The Jungle pool is drinks only and hidden in the middle of the resort by trees. The Social pool runs activities throughout the day at this adults-only resort for those who want to participate. There is also an infinity pool on the edge of the beach, and then the Preferred Club pool for those staying in that category. These are separate from the first floor swim-outs.

    The spa (hydrotherapy is included for Preferred guests) featured an outdoor circuit that included both hot and cold plunge pools, amongst other therapeutic services.

    The Preferred Club pool was the most frequented, though some images below look more vacant due to rain that rolled through during my opportunity to collect media on my short stay.

    The gym is open to every guest from 6 AM to 8 PM, and it is outfitted with Technogym equipment.

    The spa is open 8 AM to 8 PM with 17 treatment cabins and a beauty salon, and hydrotherapy is included. That last part is the headline. The hydrotherapy space is ridiculous, easily the standout of the entire property for me, and it is the kind of amenity that would make me pick this resort over a competitor down the beach. There are indoor and outdoor showers as well.

    The men’s changing room featured private showers with an option for indoor or outdoor experiences.

    Recent findings suggest that the theater seats 264 people and hosts cabaret and Mayan demonstrates. There are also pickleball courts, which I am starting to think should be required equipment at any resort that wants a younger crowd as well as padel for the European set (and growing American interest.).

    Industry observers note that secrets is an adults-only brand, and every room here comes with what the company calls Unlimited-Luxury. For a standard guest that means unlimited dining and top-shelf drinks, Wi-Fi, daytime activities and nightly entertainment, with tips and taxes included. Add 24-hour room service, a mini-bar refreshed daily (you can ask for just about anything you want in there), and pool and beach wait service for all guests.

    Recent findings suggest that the Preferred Club is an upgrade, and at this resort it is a big one because it owns the oceanfront. Secrets lists personalized check-in and check-out, afternoon hot and cold hors d’oeuvres, desserts and premium liquors, access to the Preferred Club lounge and beach bar, an upgraded mini-bar, upgraded bath amenities, butler service, Bali beds at the pool and beach reserved for club guests, and exclusive dining at the Preferred Club beach restaurant. Preferred also gives club guests exclusive access to an infinity pool and puts an oversized soaking tub on the terrace of the upgraded suites (at least with the oceanfronts).

    According to recent reports, I book a lot of Hyatt’s all-inclusives through Hyatt Privé rates, and this resort is one of 388 in the collection. Privé is Hyatt’s invitation-only program for travel advisors, so you only get the benefits when an approved advisor makes the booking, and the stay still earns World of Hyatt points and elite nights.

    The all-inclusive version of Privé looks a lot different from a Park Hyatt booking. As I wrote when Hyatt’s all-inclusive resorts joined Privé, there is no room upgrade and no breakfast benefit, since every meal is already included. At this property, Privé guests receive a $100 resort credit per stay, a welcome amenity and letter, hydrotherapy access, and early check-in and late check-out based on availability.

    Elite status matters here more than at most all-inclusives. Under World of Hyatt’s terms, Globalists get the best room available at check-in, including rooms with club access, at the resort’s discretion. Explorists are eligible for upgrades too, but not to standard suites or club rooms. Travelers who have stayed at Secrets resorts as Globalists report being designated Preferred Club guests even when they did not land in a club building, which unlocks the lounge, pool and beach areas. This was my experience on all accounts at the resort. Late checkout is 2 PM for Explorists and 4 PM for Globalists, subject to availability at resorts. It was able to honor my request for a late check-out, I did not arrive early enough to request the early check-in. Hyatt waives resort fees on eligible paid rates (at least for now) and award nights for Globalists, and on award nights only for every other tier, and Globalists also get free parking on free nights though in 2028 Globalists will have to select this as a preference. One catch is that Suite Upgrade Awards cannot be used at Secrets resorts, so you cannot lock in a suite with one here.

    In a recent development, weddings are big business here. The courtyard outside the theater is the setting, with the sunset behind it, and the resort hosts lots of them. The resort disclosed its occupancy to me but it wasn’t clear if it was for public consumption. It was shockingly high especially for a Thursday in mid-November. Over the holidays or spring break all the hotels are full but this is a period where I would have expected a lull. Still, despite being extremely full, it never felt crowded.

    For meetings and groups, the convention space measures 9,800 square feet and splits into five sections. The boardroom was occupied at the time so I couldn’t include images of that.

    Restaurants can be booked in advance through the Hyatt Inclusive Collection app, which I wish more all-inclusives offered. Nobody wants to find out at 7 PM that the restaurant they wanted is full and through the app this can be done well in advance of a guest’s arrival. The dress code in the restaurants is resort casual, though the patio does not require slacks and closed toed shoes for men, shorts are acceptable outside.

    In a recent development, the restaurants include: Portofino (Italian), Bordeaux (French), Himitsu (pan-Asian, with sushi and teppanyaki), Oceana (seafood in an open-air setting), Barefoot Grill (light lunch), Market Café (the international buffet, which I noted on site as the Marketplace), Seaside Grill (a poolside grill), and Coco Café. The bars on that list include Rendezvous in the lobby, Barracuda on the beach, a swim-up bar, a beach bar, and the Preferred Club beach bar and lounge bar. There’s also a Sports Bar and Lounge next to the theater.

    Oceana is the seafood restaurant, set in an open-air dining room with woven pendant lamps, macrame hangings and a pebble mosaic floor. I chose this for my one dinner on property during my brief stay.

    I started with the lamb croquettes, which the menu serves with yogurt and sweet chili sauce, cashews, watercress and a pickled shallot salad, and the Iberian salad with fresh mozzarella, prosciutto, rucula, toasted pistachios, balsamic and roasted peach. A crusty loaf came with the meal.

    For a main I had the coconut shrimp, served with parsley orzo pasta, coconut sauce and parmesan crispy, and finished with the mango cheesecake, which the menu plates with vanilla cream and a mango compote with honey and basil.

    It has been revealed that market Café, the international buffet I noted as the Marketplace, serves breakfast until 11:30 AM. [TO CONFIRM: lunch and dinner service at Market Café].

    Seaside Grill hosts the Preferred Club à la carte breakfast. The official dining page says breakfast there is served for Preferred Club guests only. I tried a number of dishes for lunch to report to our fine audience.

    Rendezvous sits at the heart of the property with 360-degree access, so you can walk up to it from any direction.

    Preferred Club guests get their own bar at the beach, and the Preferred Club lounge also has an indoor lounge for when the sun gets to be too much.

    My room was a Preferred Oceanfront King, a single open room with a king bed against a macrame headboard wall, rattan pendant lights, a ceiling fan, and a daybed sofa facing a marble bistro table. The balcony with jacuzzi looks straight over the beach. In the bathroom, a freestanding tub sits under a wood-slat ceiling beside a walk-in rain shower with a pebble floor and a bench. The double vanity has vessel sinks, round mirrors and a wave-textured wall, and the shower is stocked with Le Labo Bergamote 22 shampoo, conditioner and shower gel. Le Labo is a confirmed winner for me.

    I also had the chance to tour a master suites, all of which are oceanfront, and they are also available as swim-outs.

    Every first floor room is a swim-out, opening onto the pool.

    Sources indicate that secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an incredible resort that somehow felt small when you were in your building but major enough to have everything. For my stay, I used 45,000 points on a no-notice booking to offset a $1,300/night stay. I have seen rates from $560 for off-season which is without question worth it. I loved the property and I look forward to returning with more time and my wife, but the adults-only nature of the property will make it a harder stay for us to achieve.

    According to recent reports, what do you think? Have you stayed at Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres?

    American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • It has been revealed that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    It has been revealed that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The fresh lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper noted.

    Sources indicate that the airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    It has been revealed that “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano remarked in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    #99934. Breaking: Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1319 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2.
    • It has been revealed that my application was approved just before the June 30 deadline.
    • My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2. It also offered a faster track for Delta Diamond, Delta 360, AA Executive Platinum and Concierge Key members: earn 50 tiles by year-end and get Mosaic 4. That worked out to $5,000 in JetBlue flights or Paisly packages, or $50,000 on the JetBlue card, and a single Mint roundtrip to Europe could cover most of it. I already had AA Executive Platinum, so I didn’t need the status. I wanted it anyway. JetBlue was adding routes from my home airports, I fly to Boston, Latest York and Fort Lauderdale often, and the United partnership raised the possibility of benefits on both sides.

    It has been revealed that my application was approved just before the June 30 deadline. Some applicants waited up to six weeks for processing, though, and losing six weeks of a 12-week challenge is a real cost. JetBlue then added its 25-for-25 promotion on top. Visiting 25 destinations by year-end earned up to 350,000 TrueBlue points plus 25 years of Mosaic 1, which made a cheap, aggressive weekend of short hops look worth it. My plan was to finish the challenge through spend and put the points toward transatlantic and Japan trips. My one worry at the time was whether JetBlue would treat these upcoming Mosaics well enough to keep them flying with it.

    My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW). I occasionally also fly from Fort Lauderdale or Miami when it makes sense. But Pittsburgh had just flights to Boston for some of last year, before adding Fort Lauderdale to fill the Spirit gap and then Latest York JFK competing with Delta, and more broadly to the New York market, United and American with more than enough flights. From Fort Myers, it’s Boston of JFK.

    I flew once to Boston on JetBlue but at the time, it had not yet debuted a domestic first class, a better seat selection included in my fare was the only real enhancement to the short flight of just over 80 minutes. I’ll cover other reasons why I wasn’t able to fly the carrier more, but given that I am not in Newly introduced York, Boston, or Fort Lauderdale full time, every flight I take has a connection and it’s not particularly on-the-way for me. For example, if heading south to Florida, Charlotte, Atlanta, or even Washington Dulles make more sense than Boston or New York but when heading west at all, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Denver are all obviously better options.

    Even to Europe, there’s not a material advantage with limited schedules and limited footprint on the continent. For trips to Paris given that I will have to connect anyway, I have more options on any other carrier through east coast hubs than with JetBlue on its metal not to mention partner networks.

    In a recent development, most recently, I had a flight to Cancun and with airport time, flight time and connections, it’s faster to fly out of Miami or Fort Lauderdale. But JetBlue had fewer flights for more money and far more miles than with American. Outside of the northeast corridor or based in South(east) Florida, I couldn’t make it make sense.

    I’m heading to Europe for a meeting next week and I will finally have a chance to try Mint. This will constitute two of my longest flights with JetBlue ever. I haven’t heard many negative comments about JetBlue Mint, and I have high expectations. It’s hard to get excited about another American or United flight in business class solely because I have flown those so often and there’s little new there.

    I’ll get a chance to try a reasonably long three-hour flight domestically to see how it differs from my prior JetBlue experience. Then, assuming flights are on time, I should have a chance to try the newly introduced BlueHouse, a first for me. Following that is a long haul flight in Mint and I am looking forward to the experience.

    In a recent development, statistically, I can’t see a reason that I try for Mosaic again, but who knows? The experience could change what appears to be a clear analytical decision for me at this point.

    One of the biggest reasons I secure status via flying/spending/staying is to redeem systemwide upgrades (or suite upgrades in the case of hotels.) I’ll fully admit that upon receiving approval for the challenge last year, I hadn’t even considered that Mint certificates would work differently than other upgrade certificates in the industry. One upgrade certificate is worth an upgrade (if available.) United uses “Plus Points” but it feels clearer that there will be some variability in what’s required to move between the cabins.

    For this particular trip, JetBlue wanted two upgrade certificates in one direction, and four on another. Thankfully, I had taken the upgrade option every time I achieved a choice to select a benefit, but had I chosen something else assuming that I’d only need two Move to Mint certificates (as I would with American for example) I would have come up short.

    I covered how much spending is required to achieve top tier status and its associated benefits in recent posts. This was in response to United’s move to require $480,000 in annual spending (by credit card only) to achieve United 1K status. Assuming that along the way loyalty points are taken and annual Mosaic bonuses are applied to cardholders, JetBlue is above American at $225,000 in spend for Mosaic 4 vs. American’s net of $164,000 for Executive Platinum with just two systemwide upgrades, or $214,000 with six. The difference is that those six upgrades apply for the full-one-way on a single certificate.

    It has been revealed that I spent time trying to figure out why one way charged four Move to Mint vs two and in the end, it didn’t really matter. I can nearly upgrade my entire family of four on American vs a single roundtrip for myself. For what it’s worth, the base cost was also more expensive with JetBlue than American for which I had upgrades available.

    Recent findings suggest that I have the qualified business spend to earn Mosaic 4 every year, but the value of its perks aren’t even close to the rest of the market. And for what JetBlue expects in spend compared to what I could earn elsewhere is uncompetitive.

    And as a side note, the fixed rate of JetBlue points (about 1.4¢/each) is unimpressive but for most of the attempts I tried to use them throughout the year both domestically and internationally, they proved of little value. A lack of partners is much the same. I looked at a redemption in Mint on my flights to Europe and though I had more than 220,000, it was an insufficient balance for the simple roundtrip. For context, I took United a few years ago on miles and redeemed 160,000 roundtrip (this year was available at 176,000 roundtrip) and multiple times in the last 24 months on American at or around 115,000 roundtrip. Miles aren’t worth enough, they aren’t flexible enough, and there aren’t enough partners to fill gaps in the JetBlue map.

    I had higher expectations for JetBlue based on the experiences of my peers. I think its equipment is excellent, but widespread first class availability is a necessity. The limited utility of Move to Mint certificates were the nail in the coffin and the usability of the miles didn’t help. But even then, I really want to love and fly JetBlue, and I am willing to go a little out of my way to use them. But I’m not willing to fly backwards for fewer flights at a higher cost.

    Toxic Lufthansa Aims 1,000 Job Cuts But Cannot Explain Which Jobs Will Go

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs as management warns that its turnaround is falling short.
    • According to an internal letter to employees, Lufthansa management plans to cut approximately 1,000 full-time positions across its two main hubs.
    • Recent findings suggest that the letter, signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and his fellow board members, describes an airline struggling to become competitive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs as management warns that its turnaround is falling short. The financial problems are real, but I am skeptical that another vaguely defined job-cut announcement will help an airline that desperately needs to make peace with its employees in order to ultimately succeed.

    According to an internal letter to employees, Lufthansa management plans to cut approximately 1,000 full-time positions across its two main hubs.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter, signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and his fellow board members, describes an airline struggling to become competitive. Management reported an adjusted operating loss of €180 million for the first nine months of 2026, an average of €20 million per month. It cited high fuel costs, the Middle East conflict, and nine strike days among the pressures on the business. Management also acknowledged shortcomings in costs, efficiency, and productivity.

    But several basic details remain unclear:.

    (That last point is particularly important).

    The pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit responded sharply, accusing management of using an ominous but imprecise announcement to pressure employees as labor negotiations remain unresolved. The union wants answers about which jobs are affected and whether these are additional reductions. It also argues that management must take responsibility for its own operational and strategic decisions.

    According to recent reports, ground-staff union Verdi has raised similar concerns. Proposed savings include consolidating technical and administrative work currently performed separately within the organization. There may be a sensible case for that, but telling employees that 1,000 positions will disappear without explaining where or how is an excellent way to spread anxiety far beyond the people ultimately affected….

    I keep thinking about my Lufthansa A340-600 flight from Frankfurt to Washington earlier this year.

    Industry observers note that it was a superb flight, despite a business class seat that was well behind the competition. The improved food and bedding helped, but one of the main reasons I enjoyed it so much was the crew.

    Sources indicate that the flight attendants were friendly and engaging: the flight attendant working my side was so pleasant. I also sensed pride in delivering the improved onboard service, even though the fresh service flow created more work.

    Those employees gave me a reason to look forward to flying Lufthansa again.

    That anecdote certainly does not establish how many employees Lufthansa needs or whether its current labor agreements are sustainable (and this announcement does not suggest any crew positions are being cut). But my experience illustrates something management should remember as it tries to rebuild the business: good employees can make passengers want to come back, even when the seat itself is nothing special. And “happy employees make happy customers” include ground staff, lounge staff, and customer service folks too.

    In a recent development, lufthansa has published its latest proposal to the pilot union, offering the prospect of up to 1,000 cockpit hires by 2033 and up to 150 additional captain promotions annually. In exchange, it seeks changes to compensation and productivity. The proposal also includes one-time payments for 2027 and 2028, with salary increases beginning in 2029.

    Industry observers note that those prospective hires are a separate issue from the proposed hub job cuts. The different figures concern different roles and timeframes.

    Management should not have to accept every union demand and employees also have an interest in a financially viable airline: reaching an agreement will require concessions. But Lufthansa must find a way to make peace with its workforce. The latest announcement has already inflamed matters, and I struggle to see how leaving so much uncertainty helps either side reach an agreement.

    Sources indicate that if Lufthansa can eliminate unnecessary duplication while protecting the operation and treating affected employees fairly, it should be clear about it. I want Lufthansa to succeed. My A340 flight reminded me how good it can be. I would hate to see the enthusiasm I encountered onboard become another casualty of the never-ending conflict between management and labor.

    Lufthansa aims to cut 1,000 full-time positions in Frankfurt and Munich, but has yet to publicly explain several essential details, including whether those reductions are part of an existing program.

    Cost control is necessary, especially as market uncertainty and high oil prices continue. But so is a workforce willing to help deliver the airline that Lufthansa wants passengers to pay a premium to fly. My recent experience demonstrated how much its employees contribute, and I hope management can find a path to profitability that gives those employees a reason to remain invested in its success. Lufthansa is in desperate need of strong leadership…I’ll just leave it at that.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

    But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

    Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

    We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

    The answer was a resounding yes.

    According to recent reports, mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

    Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

    In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

    They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:.

    Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a fresh card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

    By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a newly introduced one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

    The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

    Next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

    Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

    However, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a new card to diversify her rewards?

    With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a new card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

    And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

    Recent findings suggest that she’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her fresh card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

    Recent findings suggest that “I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table.".

    Our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

    Recent findings suggest that while Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

    Denver opted for a latest cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

    She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

    After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

    One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”.

    Everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

    In a recent development, one went with a new travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

    All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

    This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

    Don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s newly introduced ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five fresh air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it promptly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, mentioned Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz noted the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    It has been revealed that senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz stated that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., noted after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    It has been revealed that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Recent findings suggest that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    According to recent reports, “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he noted. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    In a recent development, he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy stated, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he noted that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create concerns in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    Sources indicate that the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford mentioned Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Recent findings suggest that bedford remarked he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #99925. Latest Update: Mother Notes Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

    Latest Update: Mother Notes Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A mother says Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats.
    • In a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL).
    • She says she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that A mother says Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

    In a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

    She says she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.

    “I explained that she’s two and cannot sit by herself. Their solution? Tell me it was my responsibility to ask other passengers to switch seats.”.

    When commenters questioned whether she had purchased basic economy or failed to select seats, she clarified that she had booked Comfort+. After checking her original confirmation, she added:.

    It has been revealed that “I just looked and it was definitely Delta. I have 3 flight / time changes – I originally booked us in 15 D / 15 E / 15 F – we ended up in 15 F / 15 A / 16 A.”.

    This remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

    According to recent reports, I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

    Industry observers note that it is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

    But a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

    I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

    I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

    Recent findings suggest that A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

    That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

    In a recent development, an agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

    The ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

    The published Delta family seating policy states:.

    “Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

    Industry observers note that parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

    It has been revealed that selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

    Industry observers note that if a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

    This is called “gardening” your reservation.

    A mother claims Delta assigned her toddler a separate seat and left her to ask other passengers to move, despite originally booking seats together in Comfort+. We have only her account, but the underlying expectation is reasonable: a two-year-old should sit beside a parent, and the airline should help arrange that.

    According to recent reports, other passengers deserve respect for their seat choices too. Resolving the issue before boarding protects everyone from an awkward confrontation that should never have been necessary….

    #99924. The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2248 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
    • According to recent reports, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
    • It has been revealed that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

    According to recent reports, take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

    It has been revealed that as we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

    Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

    In a recent development, I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

    Last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

    Breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

    Industry observers note that my parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

    It has been revealed that finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

    I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I mentioned to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

    Industry observers note that newly introduced York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

    As a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with big hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

    People tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also big and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

    I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

    From bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

    In a recent development, on our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

    So we’ve adopted a fresh philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

    This may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up plans to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a newly introduced majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a newly introduced majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    Industry observers note that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    It has been revealed that “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    In a recent development, sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she stated.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday remarked at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    In a recent development, “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., remarked Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    According to recent reports, several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    Sources indicate that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    According to recent reports, “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he mentioned. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    Industry observers note that “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but remarked, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    Industry observers note that “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he noted. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    It has been revealed that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    Recent findings suggest that “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan noted.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    Sources indicate that “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Airline Elite Status So Close, Yet So Far: The Drawback To Being A Free Agent

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me.
    • According to recent reports, I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement.
    • Sources indicate that and sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me. But there are some days I wonder….

    According to recent reports, I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement. But it’s not just that. The food has improved and service has been great..flight attendants appear happy (they have a contract after all) and the operation has also been good: my personal on-time arrival rate with United is over 90% while it hovers at around 50% for American.

    Sources indicate that and sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket. This flight was from Chicago to Los Angeles and I just missed the upgrade to first class as a Gold…had I been Platinum, I would have scored an upgrade.

    I’m close…not that I’m projected to spend $5K in the last month of the year on United airfare…but it is conceivably within reach. And in the next month I’m flying Aer Lingus, American, Delta, JetBlue, KLM, and United….maybe even more.

    And having Premier Platinum status would certainly help with some upgrades and I’d put the PlusPoints to use….

    But then I pinch myself and think I’m actually only 2/3 there with 1/12 of the year left…and to spend all that money on United instead of flying the carriers and routings and times that work best for me (mostly in premium cabins…) just doesn’t make sense.

    Sources indicate that so I return to reality and think, no, the status just isn’t worth it and if I really need the premium cabin seat, I’ll pay for it. And the irony is that the majority of my flights this year have been in premium cabins and to reach top-tier status you have to essentially buy premium cabin fares anyway or else you will never spend enough. So what’s the point? Free baggage? Extra legroom seats for the family? I don’t find that worthwhile.

    So I guess the bottom line is that by splitting my loyalty this year I’ll make Gold on American and Gold on United (nothing on Alaska, Delta, or JetBlue, though I have flown them all) whereas I could have rather easily made Platinum on United had I been a bit more loyal to a product that I do genuinely like.

    But no. I still think I’m making the correct choice for my circumstances.

    And yet it’s the allure of frequent flyer elite status is still somewhat enchanting….

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

    According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

    Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

    Recent findings suggest that delta noted in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

    Industry observers note that the FAA stated on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

    According to recent reports, delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg.

    The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

    As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

    Industry observers note that while resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.
